presentations.presentation_title: Full-scale Experimental Investigation of Manhole Cover Displacement Under Urban Flood Conditions
presentations.institution: Korea Institute of Civil Engineering and Building Technology
presentations.abstract: Urban flooding has become increasingly frequent due to climate change–induced extreme rainfall, posing serious risks to stormwater sewer systems. One critical but insufficiently quantified hazard is manhole cover displacement caused by rapid pressure rise under surcharged flow conditions. This study presents a full-scale experimental investigation of manhole cover displacement under varying inflow discharge and downstream blockage conditions in an urban storm sewer system. A prototype manhole cover with a diameter of 645 mm and a mass of 20 kg was installed in a 35 m test section of a 1,000 mm diameter sewer pipe. Experiments were conducted under two inflow conditions, while downstream gate opening ratios were systematically varied from 0% to 100% to simulate different blockage scenarios. Pressure transducers were installed at the manhole sump and adjacent upstream and downstream pipe sections, and pressure variations were recorded at 1 s intervals. The results show that manhole cover displacement occurs through a staged process consisting of pressure rise, partial surcharge, cover lift-off, and subsequent reverse flow. Under partially blocked conditions, surcharge developed without immediate displacement, and the manhole cover remained stable even when sustained pressures reached approximately 0.15 bar, corresponding to an equivalent load of about 106.6 kgf. Manhole cover lift-off was observed only when pressure continued to increase beyond this level under more restrictive downstream conditions. A key finding is that inflow discharge has a stronger influence on the timing of manhole cover displacement than downstream blockage. While downstream restriction controlled the magnitude of pressure buildup, higher inflow rates accelerated pressurization and reduced the time required to reach critical conditions. These findings provide rare full-scale experimental evidence of the hydraulic mechanisms leading to manhole cover displacement and offer practical insights for improving safety assessment and design criteria for urban stormwater sewer systems under extreme rainfall.

presentations.presentation_title: Poleward Migration of Western North Pacific Tropical Cyclones and Non-stationary Extreme Rainfall in East Asia
presentations.abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) in the Western North Pacific have exhibited notable poleward migration and changing characteristics under climate change, altering their impacts on rainfall across East Asia. Using TC and daily precipitation data from 1979–2024, this study examines trends in TC migration, intensity, and translation speed, and their influence on regional and extreme precipitation. While overall TC frequency, lifespan, and translation speed have declined, high-intensity TCs have intensified and persisted longer, contributing to increased extreme rainfall in coastal East Asia. A non-stationary extreme value framework incorporating TC characteristics and climate variability further reveals heightened risks of TC-induced extreme precipitation. These findings underscore growing vulnerability of East Asian coastal regions and the need for climate-resilient risk assessment.

presentations.presentation_title: A Preliminary Study on Soft Sensing of Flood Extent along River Corridors Using Combined Satellite Observations in a Dam-Regulated River System
presentations.abstract: Extreme rainfall events in dam-regulated river systems often lead to rapid changes in flood extent along river corridors, while direct satellite observations of such events remain temporally sparse. This study presents a preliminary investigation into the feasibility of soft sensing flood extent by integrating multi-source satellite observations in a dam-regulated river system, with Jinju City, South Korea, located downstream of the Namgang Dam, selected as the study area. Satellite-based flood observations derived from Sentinel-1 SAR imagery were used to delineate flood inundation extent along river corridors during major rainfall events, while Sentinel-2 optical data were employed to distinguish temporary inundation from permanent water bodies. Concurrently, GPM IMERG satellite rainfall data were analyzed to characterize the spatio-temporal patterns of rainfall forcing associated with each event. By comparing the timing and spatial distribution of satellite-derived rainfall and flood extent, this study examines whether rainfall information can serve as a driving signal to compensate for the temporal discontinuity of flood observations. The results indicate clear event-dependent relationships between rainfall intensity, temporal rainfall evolution, and the observed expansion and persistence of flood extent along river corridors. Validation against ground-based rain gauge measurements reveals systematic underestimation in GPM rainfall intensity, highlighting the necessity of considering bias and temporal aggregation when using satellite rainfall for soft sensing applications. Despite these limitations, the combined use of rainfall and flood observations demonstrates potential for filling temporal gaps between sparse satellite acquisitions and for diagnosing the spatio-temporal response characteristics of flood extent in a dam-regulated river system. This preliminary study suggests that satellite-based soft sensing of flood extent can provide a useful observational framework for understanding flood dynamics along regulated rivers and offers a foundation for future research toward continuous flood monitoring and early-stage flood response assessment.

presentations.presentation_title: Bias-corrected Two-step Assimilation of Satellite Water Surface Elevation and Discharge for Large-scale River Reanalysis
presentations.abstract: Recent satellite missions enable observation or estimation of water surface elevation (WSE) and discharge (Q) which can be assimilated in large-scale river model. WSE is observed with high accuracy but depends on unknown riverbed elevation. Q is independent of riverbed elevation but more uncertain. There has been insufficient discussion and systematic verification regarding how to integrate WSE and Q. Here we investigate how these complementary observations can be combined to improve river reanalysis. WSE from multiple satellite missions and Q from SWOT was assimilated into the CaMa-Flood river model using Local Ensemble Transform Kalman Filter. To address riverbed elevation uncertainty, Normalized WSE (NomWSE) is assimilated. We also test a two-step assimilation approach, in which discharge is first assimilated to update the mean and variance of river storage, and the corrected statistics are used to assimilate NomWSE. Four cases were conducted over the Mississippi River Basin, differing only in the assimilated variables; (a) NomWSE (b) Q (c) NomWSE and Q simultaneously without statistical correction, and (d) with statistical correction. The results were evaluated against in-situ Q observations. Performance was quantified using IMI KGE , which measures improvements in Kling–Gupta Efficiency relative to the open-loop experiment. The results are as follows. Assimilation of Q alone improved KGE at 89% of the observation sites. However, the proportion of notable improvements was smaller than in case (d), suggesting the importance of NomWSE assimilation. Additionally, The distribution of IMI KGE is systematically shifted toward positive values in case (d) from case (c), indicating statistical correction through prior Q assimilation effectively reduced biases. This study is the first to explicitly evaluate a statistically corrected two-step assimilation framework combining satellite-derived WSE and Q in a large-scale river model. Future work will focus on the optimization of parameters to reconstruct not only discharge but also water depth and surface elevation.

presentations.presentation_title: Linking Riparian Corridors: A QGIS-Based Network Planning For Water Quality Improvement And Flood Mitigation In The Upper Marikina Watershed
presentations.abstract: Land-use conversion and urban expansion degraded riparian ecosystems. This causes declination of water quality and increases community vulnerability to flooding. Riparian corridors help in filtering sediments, stabilizing soils, and regulating water floods. The Philippines experience an average of 20 typhoons a year which results in catastrophic damages and loss of lives. This natural disaster causes severe flooding, particularly in the lowlands and built-up areas. Marikina, a progressively developing city, is highly susceptible to flooding. It is historically and geographically a low-lying area and is adjacent to the country’s prominent river, the Marikina River. Its abundance with hydrological networks and riparian corridors could be a natural way to reduce flood, but human activities and land use changes diminishes their role as natural barriers. This study aims to link riparian corridors within the Upper Marikina Watershed, a major upstream component of the Marikina River Basin that regulates water from the Sierra Madre mountain ranges to upland and lowland communities in the metro, through QGIS-based network planning, integrating sustainable strategies and interventions for water quality improvement and flood mitigation. The research analyzes and prioritizes areas for protection, improvement, and connectivity which supports both environmental preservation and disaster risk reduction. The findings of the study presents valuable reference to improve watershed planning and management.

presentations.presentation_title: The Use of C-band Sar and Machine Learning to Estimate Water Level and River Discharge
presentations.abstract: The increasing frequency of extreme rainfall and flood driven by climate change has highlighted the demand for reliable approaches to monitor flooding. In South Korea, river stages are routinely measured using telemeter, yet the sparse and uneven distribution of gauges leaves large portions of catchments ungauged. To overcome these constraints, this study utilized machine learning to estimates river stage and discharge from Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data. Sentinel-1 SAR provides weather-independent observations, and its backscatter sensitivity to surface roughness makes it well suited for hydrological applications. This study utilized a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model that integrates σ⁰ VH , σ⁰ VV , local incidence angle, and day of year as predictors. Among the various inputs, the best combination was selected using Fisher’s chi-square test, and model accuracy was assessed with correlation coefficient (R), root mean square error (RMSE), and mean absolute error (MAE). Overall result of river stage estimation showed the R ranged from 0.20 to 0.79, RMSE from 0.12 to 0.54m, and MAE from 0.08 to 0.44m. The wide range of statistical performance was highly dependent on the degree of influence from nearby hydraulic infrastructure. In order to improve the statistical performance, separate LSTM was developed by dividing stage observations below and above the median to investigate the improvement. Overall result 6 out of 11 stations showed improvement in RMSE and MAE. This study demonstrated the potential of SAR-driven deep learning to enhance hydrological monitoring across ungauged basin. Acknowledgement: This work was supported by Korea Environment Industry & Technology Institute (KEITI) through R&D Program for Innovative Flood Protection Technologies against Climate Crisis Program, funded by Korea Ministry of Environment(MOE)(RS-2023-00218873). This work also was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea(NRF) grant funded by the Korea government(MSIT)(RS-2024-00416443).

presentations.presentation_title: Integrating Spatial Weights Into Random Forest to Downscale Grace (-fo) Data to Quantify Anthropogenic and Climatic Drivers of Groundwater Depletion
presentations.abstract: Disentangling anthropogenic and climatic drivers of groundwater depletion is essential for sustainable water management. We present a novel downscaling methodology that addresses the critical challenge of spatial heterogeneity in coarse-scale Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) and its Follow-On (GRACE-FO) data. Accurately capturing this heterogeneity is essential for assessing severe depletion at the local scale, particularly in agricultural plains like the North China Plain (NCP). Aspatial machine learning approaches, such as the global random forest (GRF) model, limit the ability to capture spatial heterogeneity when downscaling GRACE (-FO) data. To address this, we propose a Geographically Weighted Random Forest (GWRF) model, integrating spatial weighting into the GRF algorithm to downscale groundwater storage anomalies (GWSAs) to 0.1° resolution over the NCP (2003-2025). The GWRF model outperforms the GRF model, increasing R 2 from 0.957 (GRF: training) and 0.73 (GRF: testing) to 0.999 (GWRF: training) and 0.897 (GWRF: testing). The high-resolution GWSAs output exhibits good correlation (r = 80) with independent in-situ groundwater measurements, enhancing its credibility. The downscaled data reveal significant groundwater depletion in the Piedmont Plain (PP: -13.42 mm/yr), Yellow River Plain (YRP: -13.25 mm/yr), Hai River Plain (HRP: -12.68), and a moderate depletion in the Coastal Plain (CP: -5.98 mm/yr) sub-regions of the NCP. We then employed a two-stage Generalized Additive Model (GAM) to quantitatively attribute the downscaled GWSAs. The analysis decisively shows anthropogenic factors are the dominant drivers, explaining 69-83% of depletion through cropland expansion, increased vegetation water use (NDVI), and population growth. In contrast, climatic variables (downward shortwave radiation, precipitation, and sea surface temperature) account for only 7-12%. This work demonstrates how geographically-aware machine learning combined with rigorous statistical attribution offers clear evidence that water resource strategies must focus on managing human demand to mitigate groundwater depletion in stressed aquifers.

presentations.presentation_title: Bias Correction and Datum Harmonisation of Swot River Water Level Observations in Data-scarce Indian Basins
presentations.abstract: Conventional satellite altimetry missions such as ERS, ENVISAT, TOPEX/Poseidon, and JASON have supported river water level monitoring but are constrained by coarse spatial resolution, sparse spatial coverage, long revisit times (10 to 35 days), and reliance on in-situ calibration for discharge estimation. Launched in December 2022, the Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission is the first satellite dedicated to global surface water monitoring. Using Ka-band radar interferometry, SWOT provides high resolution observations of key hydrological variables, including water surface elevation, extent, river width, and slope, with a 20.9 day repeat cycle. In India, hydrological assessments are limited by sparse in situ data, short and discontinuous records, and inconsistent reference datums and very few studies have been attempted in this direction. This study evaluates actual SWOT observations over India using gauge data. Fifteen-minute discharge and water surface elevation records were temporally aligned with real SWOT overpass time. To address challenges posed by short time series and datum inconsistencies, this study examines multiple bias correction techniques and simple large-scale datum harmonisation approaches. After the correction, 96.4% of the stations showed error reduction. Median improvement across the stations was 41 percent. SWOT had a higher number of observations up to 7 at higher latitudes. The results show a clear improvement in agreement between satellite-derived and in-situ observations following bias correction, though uncertainties related to record length and methodological assumptions remain. Despite these limitations, the corrected SWOT datasets demonstrate strong potential for hydrological applications such as flood inundation mapping, discharge estimation in ungauged basins, and validation of hydrodynamic flood models, highlighting SWOT’s value for both operational and research applications in data-scarce regions. The developed framework lays a strong foundation for easy correction of future altimetry missions as well.

presentations.presentation_title: Integrating Topographic Wetness Index with Sentinel-1 SAR Backscatter for Improving Soil Moisture Estimation at Micro-watershed Scales
presentations.abstract: Improved soil moisture estimation at local scale can be beneficial for modeling hydrological processes and estimating agricultural water availability in monsoon-dominated regions of Eastern India. While Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) backscatter is widely used to estimate surface soil moisture, but its response is often influenced by the movement and accumulation of moving water controlled by local topography. This study aims to assess performance of integrated model with Digital Elevation Model (DEM) derived Topographic Wetness Index (TWI) and C-band SAR backscatter, whether it can improve soil moisture estimation at the micro-watershed scale. The study is conducted over selected micro-watersheds in Hindol, Dhenkanal, Odisha, covering an area of more than 12 km², where field-monitoring of soil moisture and groundwater levels is performed at weekly time step for hydrologic analysis. The PR2/6 soil moisture profile probes are used to monitor data during December 2023 to January 2025, at multiple depths in the soil layer. Primarily, the observed surface soil moisture at 10 cm depth is explored for correlation with C-band SAR sensitivity. Terrain attributes are derived from a high-resolution 5 m DEM to characterise spatial wetness patterns. Sentinel-1 Interferometric Wide (IW) mode Ground Range Detected (GRD) products are analysed for pre-monsoon, monsoon, and post-monsoon periods following standard SAR preprocessing. Relationships among observed soil moisture, SAR backscatter, and TWI are then modeled using regression-based approaches. The study demonstrates that integrating terrain information enhances the interpretability of SAR-derived soil moisture and enhances estimation of soil moisture in data-scarce regions that do not have dense network of in-situ observations.

presentations.presentation_title: Optimization of Evacuation Routing Under Road Inundation Scenarios Caused by the Namgang Dam Failure
presentations.abstract: This study aims to develop a realistic dynamic evacuation route model by quantitatively analyzing inundation characteristics and evacuation feasibility under a hypothetical failure scenario of the Namgang Dam in Jinju City, South Korea. Flood propagation was simulated using a two-dimensional unsteady flow analysis with HEC-RAS 2D, and key hydraulic parameters, including inundation depth, flow velocity, and flood arrival time, were derived. The hydraulic results were integrated with a GIS-based network analysis to comprehensively evaluate evacuation safety, accessibility, and efficiency while explicitly accounting for inundated road conditions. The study area was classified into five zones (Zones A–E), with detailed analysis focused on Zone A, a low-lying urban area adjacent to the Namgang River characterized by extremely short flood arrival times of less than 30 minutes. The results indicate that river-adjacent sections (R-01–R-03) experience inundation depths exceeding 10 m, making pedestrian evacuation infeasible for all age groups. In contrast, urban and elevated sections (R-04–R-07) provide sufficient evacuation time, achieving a 100% evacuation success rate across all age groups. Accordingly, vertical evacuation to rooftops of high-rise buildings is proposed as the most practical strategy for low-lying areas where horizontal evacuation is not possible. Furthermore, a multi-criteria analysis incorporating flood arrival time, inundation depth, and road accessibility revealed that conventional shortest-distance evacuation routes are unsuitable under real flood conditions. Applying alternative routes toward northern highlands improved evacuation success rates by approximately 35%. By integrating hydrodynamic modeling with spatial network analysis, this study overcomes the limitations of static evacuation planning and provides a practical framework for non-structural flood risk management and urban disaster mitigation planning.

presentations.presentation_title: A Historical Stress Test of Megacity Flood-system Failure Revealing the Return-period Paradox
presentations.abstract: Catastrophic coastal-city floods are often attributed to rare extremes in rainfall or storm tide, yet disasters can occur when moderate drivers synchronize in time within a hydraulically constrained urban delta. We revisit the 1905 Shanghai flood, widely described as a black swan urban disaster with nearly 25,000 deaths, as a stress test of megacity flood-system failure. Using historical typhoon track and pressure observations, we reconstruct storm forcing and drive a two-dimensional hydrodynamic model configured with early-twentieth-century river networks, coastline, bathymetry, and embankments. Long-term records show that two antecedent daily rainfall pulses of only ~2-year and ~5-year return periods, together with an approximately ~10-year storm tide, nonetheless produced modeled inundation over ~73% of Shanghai, with >1 m depths across large districts. Factorial experiments attribute this severity to asymmetric preconditioning by the later rainfall pulse, tide-locking under spring-tide timing that suppresses drainage (neap-tide timing reduces inundation to ~50% and lowers high-end depths by ~1 m), and defense-driven redistribution that shifts exposure spatially. Together, these results formalize a return-period paradox for coastal megacities and motivate state-dependent, temporally explicit flood-risk metrics and early-warning systems that track multi-day hazard trajectories rather than isolated peaks.

presentations.presentation_title: Urban Drainage Response to Elevated River Water Levels: Centralized Vs Distributed Storage
presentations.abstract: Urban flooding can intensify markedly when rainfall-driven internal flooding coincides with elevated river stages that impose external hydraulic controls. Rising river water levels (stage) may submerge urban drainage outfalls, increase hydraulic heads within pipe networks, and trigger cascading surcharging, manhole overflows, and surface inundation. This study aims to assess how downstream river-level boundary conditions modulate urban flooding and how the spatial configuration of gray infrastructure—conceptualized here as centralized versus distributed storage—affects flood response under compound forcing. A scenario-based modeling framework is developed by combining representative rainfall events (e.g., design rainfall of multiple return periods) with a set of downstream river-level boundary conditions spanning typical to high-stage conditions. For each scenario, an urban drainage model is executed to quantify flood hazard metrics such as total flood volume, number of flooding nodes, and flood duration, following established sensitivity-analysis practices that relate downstream water levels to urban flooding behavior. Gray infrastructure alternatives are represented as (i) a centralized configuration concentrating storage capacity at limited downstream locations and (ii) a distributed configuration allocating storage across multiple upstream and midstream locations within the drainage system. The performance of each configuration is compared across the river-level–rainfall scenario matrix, with attention to potential non-linear amplification of flooding under elevated boundary stages and to shifts in the distribution of vulnerable nodes. The evaluation follows established detention-tank performance assessment practices in urban drainage modeling. The results are expected to provide actionable insights into when distributed gray storage may offer greater robustness than centralized measures under high river stages, thereby supporting planning and design of urban flood mitigation strategies in river-influenced cities. Acknowledgements : This work was supported by Korea Environmental Industry & Technology Institute(KEITI) through Climate Resilient R&D Project for Water-Related Disaster Managements, funded by Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment(MCEE)(RS-2024-00398012).

presentations.presentation_title: Flood Analysis of the Uji River Under Climate Change and Evaluation of Backwater Effects at the Three-river Confluence
presentations.abstract: Due to the impact of global warming, the risk of unprecedented floods has increased,and numerous studies have addressed issues related to climate change. However,detailed flood analyses that incorporate climate change while considering historicalcontext, current issues, and focusing on specific river basins remain insufficient.This study targets the Uji River in Kyoto Prefecture and the downstream three-riverconfluence (Uji, Katsura, and Kizu Rivers). The study area includes the Former OguraPond region, characterized by a basin-shaped topography and possibly influenced bybackwater effects from the confluence. In addition, residential areas have expanded overyears, and several schools are currently located in the vicinity.The objectives of this study are to clarify: 1) the flood risk of the Uji River under climatechange, 2) the behavior of floodwaters influenced by the basin-shaped FormerOgura Pond, and 3) backwater effects originating from the confluence. Using thesoftware “iRIC-Nays2D Flood”, we conducted two types of analyses: 1) flood simulation ofthe Uji River alone considering the impact of climate changes, and 2) analyses ofbackwater effects and flood behavior at the three-river confluence. For the input data,5-m mesh topographic data and river discharge data from Water Information System ofMinistry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism (MLIT) were used. Climatechange scenarios were created with reference to the future change of peak riverdischarge during flood events simulated by MLIT for RCP2.6 and RCP8.5.The influence of climate change was evaluated based on inundation area, floodwaterbehavior, and water level variations.Results indicate that inundation area increases non-linearly as discharge increases.Furthermore, floodwater flows into the basin-shaped depression of the Former OguraPond, resulting in significant inundation depth. Further detailed findings andsubsequent results will be presented at the conference.

presentations.presentation_title: When the Desert Floods: Climate Change, Infrastructure, and Flood Inundation in Cooper Creek
presentations.institution: Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation
presentations.abstract: Flood inundation modelling in arid and semi-arid regions is challenging due to sparse data, episodic flows, and complex hydraulics. Yet dryland floods sustain ecological processes and pose risks to infrastructure, making robust models critical for understanding climate-driven changes and informing adaptation planning.Cooper Creek, one of the world’s largest unregulated dryland systems, exemplifies these challenges. Its low-gradient floodplain features anastomosing ephemeral channels and long flood residence times. Large events can take months to drain, producing widespread inundation that sustains floodplain productivity but threatens gas extraction infrastructure.A two-dimensional hydrodynamic model (MIKE21 FM) covering the Queensland and South Australian floodplain (~30,000 km2) was developed using LiDAR-derived topography, waterhole bathymetry, soil characteristics, rainfall, evapotranspiration, gauged flows, and satellite-derived inundation for historical flood events. The calibrated model reproduces observed inundation patterns and was used as a baseline to assess two groups of scenarios: infrastructure developments (including roads, tracks, borrow pits, and well pads) and future climate conditions. Climate scenarios were derived from 37 Global Climate Models, using the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentiles of projected rainfall, evapotranspiration, and runoff to represent drier, medium, and wetter futures. Model outputs were presented through interactive online story maps, integrating hydrodynamic simulations with geospatial layers, explanatory text, and visualisations of flood metrics such as inundation extent, depth, duration, and connectivity, enabling accessible exploration of scenario-based flood risks by diverse stakeholders.Results demonstrate that projected changes in climate forcing significantly influence flood inundation responses, leading to shifts in flood extent, duration, and connectivity. Infrastructure exerts a comparatively smaller influence, primarily modifying flow pathways at local scales. This highlights how dryland flood risk is shaped by the combined, but uneven, influence of climate variability and human modification. Beyond Cooper Creek, the study provides transferable insights for flood risk assessment and management in other data-sparse arid river systems globally.

presentations.presentation_title: Assessing The Effects Of Typhoon Modification’s Intensity and Timing On Flood Damage Mitigation In Japan: An Impact-based Ensemble Forecasting Study Of Typhoon Hagibis (2019)
presentations.abstract: Typhoon Hagibis (2019), one of the most powerful storms to strike Japan in recent years, caused widespread flooding and severe damage. Impact-based forecasting play a critical role in planning effective mitigation measures and enhancing disaster preparedness and responses. In this study, we employ the Integrated Land Simulator (ILS) coupled with the Nonhydrostatic Icosahedral Atmospheric Model (NICAM) to evaluate the effects of typhoon intensity modification on flood damage mitigation associated with Typhoon Hagibis. To systematically assess uncertainties in typhoon forecasts, we conducted ensemble simulations consisting of a control run and ten ensemble members. The results indicate that the spatial distribution of heavy rainfall and flooding is strongly influenced by the typhoon track. Westward shifts in the typhoon track led to expanded heavy rainfall and flooding expanded over southwestern Japan, whereas eastward shifts resulted in increased impacts over central Japan, particularly in the densely populated Kanto region. To further investigate the effects of typhoon intensity modification on flood damage mitigation, the central pressure of the typhoon was artificially increased by 1 to 15 hPa at 1-hPa intervals on 10 and 11 October. These intensity modification experiments demonstrate that human intervention generally reduced heavy rainfall and flood damage across Japan. Moreover, modifications applied on October 10 produced greater reductions in both heavy rainfall and flood damage than those applied on October 11.These findings highlight the critical importance of both the intensity and timing of human intervention in influencing flood risk. By simulating different modification intensities and timings and explicitly evaluating the role of weather modification, this study advances our understanding of flood hazards and provides valuable insights for improving disaster preparedness and flood mitigation strategies.

presentations.presentation_title: Performance Assessment of High-resolution Climate Model in Simulating Extreme Precipitation and Flood-related Hazards Over the Greater Bay Area
presentations.institution: Southern University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Extreme precipitation is intensifying under climate change, posing increasing flood hazards to highly urbanized megacity clusters. The Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA), one of the most densely populated and rapidly developing regions in China, is particularly vulnerable to rainfall-induced flooding. Reliable assessment of climate model performance in such complex urban environments is therefore essential for advancing extreme precipitation research and climate change impact studies. In this study, we evaluate and compare the performance of a convection-permitting regional climate model, HadRAM3-RA1T (4km), and a coarser-resolution model, HadREM3-GA7.05 (12km), in simulating extreme precipitation and flood-related hazards over the GBA. Model simulations are assessed using high-quality station-based observations at both daily and hourly timescales, enabling a comprehensive evaluation of rainfall characteristics across multiple temporal scales. The models’ ability was examined to reproduce the spatial distribution, frequency, intensity, and temporal structure of extreme precipitation events relevant to flood generation. Results show that the 4km convection-permitting model substantially improves the representation of localized intense rainfall and spatial heterogeneity compared with the 12km simulation. However, biases in extreme-event magnitude and temporal clustering persist, indicating remaining uncertainties even at convection-permitting scales. Our findings underscore the critical importance of high-resolution climate modeling for studying extreme precipitation in megacity regions and provide valuable insights into the reliability of regional climate simulations for climate change impact and flood hazard assessments. This study contributes to a better understanding of the role of model resolution in improving extreme rainfall representation, supporting more robust climate adaptation and disaster risk reduction strategies in rapidly urbanizing regions.

presentations.presentation_title: Future Flood Hazards in Nepal: Projecting Magnitude Changes and Targeting Nature-based Mitigation.
presentations.abstract: Flood impacts in Nepal are increasing, and are projected to intensify under climate-change over the 21st century. To help mitigate this increased hazard, two of the key questions are ‘how much will the flood magnitude and frequency change?’ and ‘If we are to use catchment-based mitigation approaches, including nature-based solutions, where in the catchment should they be implemented?’ We present the results of simulation modelling in the Karnali catchment and flood-source risk mapping in the East-Rapti. Within the Karnali catchment, we used the SPHY hydrological model, coupled with 12 CMIP6 GCM ensemble members, to simulate changes in flood magnitude and frequency. This modelling was undertaken within a GLUE-based uncertainty-estimation framework. Within the East-Rapti, we mapped the most likely effective locations for implementing nature-based solutions with SCIMAP-Flood. This tool is based on catchment connectivity, land-use, rainfall patterns, and floodwater travel times to the impacted communities. The simulations for the Kanali catchment show a projected increase in the 1% annual exceedance probability flood magnitude of + 40% (P10/90: 33/48%) (medium-emissions) and + 79% (P10/90: 54/82%) (high-emissions) for 2060–2099, with rainfall-runoff contributing ≥ 90% of the additional flood water, as opposed to groundwater or glacial-melt. For the East-Rapti catchment, the SCIMAP-Flood results indicate that spatial targeting of mitigation measures in irrigated and rainfed agriculture, and the prevention of deforestation or the removal of shrubland, would be the most effective approaches. If these actions were in the upper catchment above Hetauda, or upstream of Manahari, they would have the most effective reduction in the flood peak. Overall, these tools improve our understanding of the flood hazard generation by quantifying changes in flood magnitudes and frequencies, analysing the contributions of runoff components, and mapping the critical source areas of floodwater generation. When combined, they can provide effective measures for developing flood risk management strategies.

presentations.presentation_title: Urban Flood Detection with CCTV Footages and Yolov8 Across Taiwan
presentations.abstract: As climate change intensifies, urban flash floods have become increasingly frequent due to extreme rainfall events in cities worldwide. In Taiwan, these floods occur primarily during May and June, where intense storms can trigger flooding within one hour that often recedes just as rapidly. This short duration makes real-time monitoring a significant challenge for disaster management. In this study, we collected over 3,000 CCTV stations across Taiwan during 2023 to 2025. From this extensive dataset, we utilized 194 flooding images to train a YOLOv8n model for automated detection. The results show that the model successfully screened 98% of the CCTV stations with only 2% of false alarm rate. When validated against unseen footage from the Water Resources Agency, the model correctly detected approximately 80% of flooding images. Furthermore, we applied SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to interpret the model’s decision-making process. The analysis revealed that the characteristic yellowish hue of floodwater is a critical feature identified by the YOLO model for accurate detection.

presentations.presentation_title: An Impact-based Evaluation Methodology for Identifying Manholes Contributing to Urban Underground Flooding
presentations.institution: School of Advance science and Technology Convergence, Kyungpook National University
presentations.abstract: This study proposes an impact-oriented evaluation approach to quantitatively determine the most influential manholes contributing to underground flooding within a dense urban drainage network surrounding Seoul’s SNUniv. of Education Station. An integrated modeling framework combining SWMM with a two-dimensional surface inundation model was applied to simulate multiple rainfall scenarios across a range of return periods (30–500 years) and event durations (60–180 minutes). The relative influence of individual manholes was evaluated using key hydraulic indicators, including proximity to subway entrances, timing of overflow initiation, and total overflow volume. The analysis revealed that manholes 8201, 2112, and 4100 repeatedly demonstrated high impact, acting as critical control points for flood transmission into underground spaces. Overall, the proposed framework offers a quantitative and operationally applicable basis for enhancing flood warning strategies and prioritizing manhole management within urban drainage systems.Funding This work was supported by the Technology Innovation Program (RS202400398858, Development of AI-based urban flood damage risk prediction and evaluation technology for practical use) funded By the Ministry of the Interior and Safety(MOIS, Korea), and by National Disaster Management Research Institute (NDMI), Ministry of the Interior and Safety, Republic of Korea (Project No. RS-2025-02218717).

presentations.presentation_title: Prediction of Flood and Drought Frequency Under Climate Change Based on an Online-coupling System of a Distributed Hydrological and Inundation Model
presentations.abstract: Flood damage has increased worldwide due to heavy precipitation driven by climate change. In contrast, during the summer of 2025, drought risk increased in 37 river basins across Japan as a result of a significant decrease in precipitation. These contrasting hydrological extremes highlight the importance of assessing the impacts of climate change on both the frequency and magnitude of floods and droughts. However, such assessments are often limited by the high computational cost of conventional inundation models. In this study, we applied an online-coupled system integrating a distributed hydrological model with a computationally efficient inundation model to the Shirakawa River basin, which was severely affected by the North Kyushu flood disaster in July 2012. To evaluate climate change impacts on flood and drought characteristics, we used the d4PDF large-ensemble climate dataset, considering the present climate (HPB) and a future +4 K warming scenario (hereafter referred to as F4K). The results indicate that both flood and drought frequencies are likely to increase under the F4K scenario compared to the HPB. This increase can be attributed to enhanced extreme precipitation events as well as an increase in the number of dry days under future climate conditions. Furthermore, the maximum river discharge and inundation area during flood events were projected to be larger in the F4K scenario than in the present climate. These findings suggest that climate change affects not only flood hazards associated with intense rainfall but also water resources through prolonged dry conditions. Therefore, effective climate change adaptation strategies should simultaneously address flood control and water resource management.

presentations.presentation_title: Dynamic Urban Flood Risk under Rapid Migration: Individual Adaptation and Collective Vulnerability in Phnom Penh’s Peri-Urban Floodplains
presentations.abstract: Rapid and unregulated urban expansion in Phnom Penh has intensified flood risk in low-lying peri-urban areas. New urban migrants increasingly settle on reclaimed floodplains where drainage and regulation lag behind development. This study analyses how flood hazard (H), exposure (E), vulnerability (V), and coping capacity (C) interact to shape evolving flood risk. It extends the Methods for the Improvement of Vulnerability Assessment in Europe (MOVE) framework by integrating settlement duration as a temporal dimension of risk transformation. Data come from a 560-household survey and 36 village authorities across four peri-urban communes (Sangkats). Flood hazard indicators differ significantly by settlement duration. New and mid-term migrants experience the most frequent (>5 events/year) and prolonged (>1 week) floods. Exposure correlates strongly with population growth, reflecting unplanned expansion into poorly drained floodplains. Physical vulnerability remains high among new migrants. Over half live in poor-condition, single-storey houses, and nearly one-third rent insecure dwellings. Although better educated and financially active, many face limited support from the community and Sangkat-level governance, leaving preparedness to individual initiative. Evidence shows that migrants invest in self-protection, but adaptation differs across settlement groups. Mid-term migrants demonstrate stronger adaptation through housing improvements and community integration, while new migrants remain more exposed. However, these individual efforts do not offset the systemic rise in exposure. The results illustrate a fallacy of composition. Individual households adapt rationally, yet their collective actions increase overall flood risk under weak infrastructure and governance. The study concludes that urban flood risk in Phnom Penh is dynamic, cumulative, and socially differentiated. Strengthening resilience requires coordinated drainage investment, land-use control, and inclusive flood governance that bridges household adaptation with Sangkat-level planning.

presentations.presentation_title: Analysis of River Flooding Using Particle Method with PLATEAU
presentations.abstract: In recent years, heavy rainfall disasters have been frequent in Japan, and more detailed river inundation analysis is required to predict various damage risks. Although the Euler-based grid method has been widely used for river inundation analysis in the past, the Lagrangian-based particle method has been attracting attention due to recent improvements in computer processing power, enabling the simulation of complex three-dimensional fluid behaviors without complex mesh generation. In this study, we conducted a river inundation analysis using the particle method, specifically DualSPHysics, integrated with the 3D urban models called PLATEAU provided by the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism of Japan, to visualize various factors that may cause damage risk. Focusing on the Shirakawa River basin in Kumamoto, we simulated a levee breach to examine the effectiveness of the particle method as an inundation analysis and the compatibility between the particle method and PLATEAU. The results of the analysis showed that the particle method is more effective than the grid method in visualizing the detailed behavior of inundation flows affected by buildings. Since the particle method enables three-dimensional analysis, it was possible to visualize results on vertical cross-sections perpendicular to the ground surface, extending beyond simple surface flow. Furthermore, the analysis allowed for the calculation of specific hydraulic forces acting on a wall of a building, revealing dynamic pressure fluctuations over time. This indicates that the particle method can be utilized for damage risk evaluation by combining the analysis results with building structure information. The high compatibility between PLATEAU and the particle method is expected to lead to the clarification of the relationship between urban structure and flood damage. Consequently, such analysis is expected to be applied to the evaluation of damage risk according to the arrangement and structure of buildings in various regions.

presentations.presentation_title: Impact Assessment on Alder Growth Due to Changes of Flood Inundation Characteristics Before and After River Meandering Restoration in Kushiro Mire, Hokkaido, Japan
presentations.abstract: In recent years, nature restoration projects have been implemented worldwide to preserve precious wetland environments, which also play a key role in mitigating global warming. The Kushiro Mire in Hokkaido, Japan, underwent a river meandering restoration project in 2010 for the Kushiro River, which had been straightened in the 1980s. This past straightening had resulted in the severe degradation of peat bogs to alder forests and the loss of the wetland landscape. This study analyzed temporal changes in alder forests before and after river meandering restoration using satellite imagery. This study then examined the hydrological effects on alder forest dynamics using a numerical model of river flood inundation. The satellite image analysis of the alder forest used satellite imagery from 2004 to 2023, obtained from Google Earth Engine. The flood inundation analysis was performed using the iRIC software with the Nay2D Flood solver. The topographic data used for this study were data from airborne laser surveys and regular river longitudinal and cross-sectional surveys by the national administrative body. The satellite image analysis revealed that the proportion of alder forests after the restoration decreased by 5% compared to the pre-restoration period. The flood inundation analysis indicated that the area of alder forest loss expanded upstream after the meandering restoration and that alder loss increased by 5-7%. This is because the meandering restoration increased the location and frequency of flooding on alder trees in the target wetland area. The results from both the satellite image analysis and flood model analysis were consistent, suggesting that natural restoration through river meandering could suppress alder forest proliferation. Future work will further examine changes in alder forest dynamics before and after restoration, while accounting for the characteristics of the peat soil in the wetland.

presentations.presentation_title: Large-scale Flood Modeling of the Tokyo Metropolitan Area Using Open-source Data
presentations.abstract: This study performs a large-scale flood simulation of the Tokyo metropolitan area using the shallow water equation on a supercomputer. All input data were open-source, including 5‑meter elevation data from the Geospatial Information Authority, building data from MLIT’s PLATEAU, 1‑minute rainfall observations from the Tokyo Metropolitan Government, and administrative boundaries from the Digital National Land Information. With the growing availability of sub‑meter elevation datasets from satellite and aerial LiDAR surveys, the need for high‑resolution flood modeling is increasing. However, fully representing stormwater infrastructure -such as sewer systems, underground reservoirs, subways, and commercial underground spaces -remains difficult in large‑scale simulations. Therefore, this study evaluates drainage system effects through sensitivity analysis, validated using observed water levels from the major pluvial flooding near Tokyo City University. The results show reasonable performance. Because real urban space is continuous, simulation accuracy must be assessed from both spatial resolution and drainage‑system representation. Reference: Kenichiro KOBAYASHI, High-resolution modeling of pluvial flooding throughout a metropolitan area utilizing open-source data and a supercomputer, Hydrological Research Letter (to be published)

presentations.presentation_title: Vision-enabled Flood Depth Estimation with 2d Hydrodynamic Modeling for Urban Flood Risk Mapping: Insights from Bangkok, Thailand
presentations.abstract: Accurate, timely, and spatially explicit flood-depth information is critical for real-time urban flood monitoring, emergency response, and decision-support systems. This study proposes a real-time framework that integrates vision-based flood-depth estimation with two-dimensional hydrodynamic modeling to generate dynamic urban flood inundation maps. The framework couples deep learning–based image analysis with a physically based PCSWMM 2D flood model to address the limitations associated with sparse in-situ water-level observations in complex urban environments. The proposed framework comprises two main components. First, flood depth is estimated from street-level images using the YOLO deep learning architecture. YOLO-based object detection is employed to identify vehicle wheels as reference objects with known geometric characteristics, while YOLO-based image segmentation is applied to delineate flooded areas and detect waterlines relative to the detected wheels. Flood depth is calculated from pixel-level distance measurements and converted into real-world units using geometric scaling. The vision-based flood-depth estimates demonstrate strong agreement with reference observations, indicating the reliability of the proposed image-based approach. Second, the image-derived flood-depth estimates are assimilated into a PCSWMM two-dimensional (2D) hydrodynamic model to support real-time urban flood mapping. These observations are used to calibrate, validate, and dynamically update simulated flood depths and inundation extents. The integration of vision-based observations with PCSWMM 2D enhances flood-extent representation and reduces water-depth simulation errors compared to baseline simulations without image-based data assimilation. The proposed framework demonstrates the feasibility of a real-time urban flood monitoring system that integrates CCTV and crowdsourced imagery with hydrodynamic modeling. This approach provides a scalable and cost-effective solution for near real-time flood mapping, improved situational awareness, and informed decision-making under rapidly evolving flood conditions.

presentations.presentation_title: A Holistic Framework for Assessing Hydrological Degradation Vulnerability of an Ungauged Non-perennial River: a Case Study of the Pennar River Basin, India
presentations.abstract: The hydrological degradation vulnerability (HDV) of a non-perennial river represents the progressive deterioration of its natural flow regime, characterized by shortened flow duration and reduced baseflow. When a river basin loses its capacity to store, transmit, and regulate water, its resilience to climatic variability declines and the system becomes increasingly vulnerable. This problem is especially pronounced in semi-arid and arid regions, where climatic variability, anthropogenic pressures, and geogenic hazards jointly intensify hydrological degradation. This study evaluates HDV in the Pennar River Basin, India, by integrating multiple controlling attributes: the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI), Standardized Groundwater Table Index (SGWTI), density of minor surface water bodies, groundwater–surface water head difference, and sinkhole density. The relative importance of these attributes is quantified using the Analytical Hierarchy Process. The results are validated using a newly developed depth–duration curve–based river–aquifer stress index and further cross-validated with the standardized total water storage anomaly derived from GRACE and GRACE-FO satellite observations (HI_STWSA).To improve spatial resolution, the total water storage anomaly is downscaled using machine learning techniques. Key independent predictors are identified, and the optimal model is selected using entropy-based performance metrics. The final model downscales STWSA using SPEI, SGWTI, canopy cover, and surface water pixel density, enabling a detailed assessment of spatial vulnerability patterns. The results reveal strong spatial variability in HDV across the basin. The Pennar River near Chennur, in its upstream reach, exhibits high vulnerability, primarily due to intensive groundwater extraction and extensive sinkhole development, which severely disrupts subsurface storage and flow continuity. In contrast, the downstream reach near Nellore shows comparatively lower vulnerability, reflecting reduced extraction pressure and better retention of hydrological connectivity. These findings highlight the urgent need for region-specific groundwater management strategies to mitigate hydrological degradation in non-perennial river systems under increasing climatic stress.

presentations.presentation_title: Quantifying the Impact of Land Use Change on Hydrological Processes in the Yangtze River Basin Using Deep Learning
presentations.abstract: The Yangtze River Basin, as a crucial strategic water resource region in China, is vital to the development and security of nearly 400 million people. Under the dual influence of climate change and human activities, significant changes have occurred in the land use pattern of the Yangtze River Basin, accompanied by alterations in its hydrological regimes. In recent years, extreme hydrological events have occurred frequently in the basin. Accurately quantifying the impact of land use change on river runoff is of great significance for adapting to hydrological changes. However, most existing studies focus on the effects on runoff volume or depth, failing to deeply reveal how land use change influences the intrinsic processes of runoff generation, particularly its impacts on key hydrological process characteristics such as floods, baseflow, and intra-annual distribution uniformity. This study aims to explore in depth the effects of land use change on runoff characteristics including floods, baseflow, and intra-annual unevenness coefficient, thereby refining the mechanisms through which land use change affects hydrological processes. To this end, the research employs deep learning algorithms to simulate daily-scale runoff in the Yangtze River Basin and applies a baseflow separation algorithm to partition baseflow. Based on the simulation results, the impact of land use change on runoff characteristics is quantified. The findings indicate that land use change significantly influences runoff characteristics such as floods, baseflow, and intra-annual distribution in the Yangtze River Basin. This study quantifies the effects of land use change on runoff characteristics including floods, baseflow, and intra-annual unevenness coefficient in the Yangtze River Basin. It contributes to revealing the regulatory effects of land use change on basin hydrological processes, providing a scientific basis for water resource management and conservation practices in the Yangtze River Basin.

presentations.presentation_title: Spatiotemporal Dynamics of Chlorophyll-algal Density Relationships in Large River Basins Under Climate Change
presentations.abstract: Under climate change, the frequency and intensity of algal blooms in rivers and lakes have increased. Chlorophyll is commonly used as an indicator of algal blooms; however, its relationship with algal density is not linear. Such nonlinearity may introduce uncertainty in predicting bloom intensity based on chlorophyll alone. This may affect subsequent algal bloom predictions; therefore, it is crucial to clarify the dynamic relationship between chlorophyll and algal density. This study analyzes water quality data (2021–2024) to explore the dynamic relationship between chlorophyll and algal density in six major river basins in China. This study first examined the spatiotemporal patterns of the correlation and found significant spatiotemporal differences. Subsequently, random forest models and SHAP were applied to identify key water quality indicators affecting the correlation. We further employed linear regression to categorize monitoring sites in China into four temporal patterns, providing a basis for regional LSTM modeling. Our results indicate that the correlation between chlorophyll and algal density changes with spatiotemporal variations. Nutrient concentrations and turbidity were identified as key drivers, although their effects varied among basins and years. This study shows that accounting for regional differences is essential when interpreting Chl-a-algal relationships.

presentations.presentation_title: Precipitation Thresholds and Mechanisms of Nitrogen-to-Phosphorus Ratio (N:P) Shifts under Extreme Rainfall in the Yangtze River Basin
presentations.abstract: Under global climate change, extreme precipitation events are occurring more frequently, and total nitrogen (TN) and total phosphorus (TP) in river basins exhibit asymmetric responses, altering the nutrient structure. The nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio (N:P), an important indicator of nutrient limitation in freshwater ecosystems, may undergo abrupt shifts under extreme rainfall conditions. However, the precipitation thresholds triggering these shifts and their underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Existing studies have largely focused on the responses of individual indicators, such as TN or TP, under extreme precipitation, while systematic analyses of abrupt changes in N:P are still limited. This study focuses on the Yangtze River Basin and constructs a daily-scale precipitation–water quality dataset for 2020–2024. Nonparametric PELT was applied to detect change points in the N:P time series, and correlation analysis assessed their associations with precipitation characteristics. Threshold analysis identified critical precipitation levels associated with abrupt N:P changes, and machine learning combined with SHAP interpretability analysis revealed the driving factors under varying precipitation amounts and intensities. The results provide insights into nutrient limitation transitions under extreme rainfall and support threshold-based water quality management, as well as nonpoint source pollution and eutrophication control at the basin scale.

presentations.presentation_title: Wildfire-driven Alterations to Sediment Regimes in Eastern Australia: Event-scale Evidence
presentations.abstract: Wildfires can fundamentally alter hydrological and geomorphic processes in forested catchments, often triggering pronounced changes in sediment transport and downstream water quality. Although post-fire increases in sediment and other water quality constituents have been widely reported, understanding remains limited on how fire and hydrological conditions interact to drive these responses, and their variability across catchments.Here we investigate how wildfire disturbance and short-term hydrological conditions interact to control sediment mobilization at the event scale. We apply a Bayesian hierarchical modelling framework to multi-year, high-frequency turbidity and streamflow observations from a network of forested catchments in eastern Australia. These catchments experienced a wide range of burn severities during the 2019-2020 Black Summer fires and were subsequently impacted by multiple flood events. We further examine how post-fire sediment responses vary with the extent and spatial configuration of burning, as well as key catchment characteristics.Our results indicate that severe wildfire disturbance led to clear steepening of event-scale concentration-discharge (C-Q) relationships in a substantial subset of the most severely burned catchments. This implies that sediment mobilization has been enhanced consistently across catchments which experienced more severe wildfires. In contrast, short-term hydrological conditions had modest influences on C-Q behavior, suggesting that fire-induced landscape changes dominated sediment responses in the immediate post-fire period. Notably, the strength of post-fire sediment responses did not scale simply with the overall proportion of catchment burned but appeared to depend on the spatial distribution of severe burning and forest type. These findings provide event-scale, multi-catchment evidence of how wildfire alters sediment regimes in river basins, improving understanding of post-disturbance hydrological alteration and offering insights to support sediment modelling and management in fire-affected landscapes.Keywords: wildfire, bushfire, sediment, mobilization

presentations.presentation_title: Predicting Impacts Of Land Use And Climate Changes On Salinity Risks With A Bayesian Network Model
presentations.abstract: Stream salinity is affected by multiple factors, including hydro-climatological conditions, land use types and soil properties, and remains a critical ongoing concern for many regions worldwide, including the New South Wales (NSW) portion of the Murray-Darling Basin. Although some success has been achieved at macro scales in the Murray-Darling Basin by managing stream salinity at the end of individual catchments, emerging salinity risks are observed at sub-catchment scales. This scale has received limited attention in existing risk management frameworks despite it being more relevant for targeting salinity management. Moreover, both land use changes and climate change could lead to alteration of stream salinity risks. Understanding the spatiotemporal variation of salinity risks and its dynamics under future changes in climate and land use often requires resource-intensive process-based modelling for every sub-catchment, which is highly challenging. This work focuses on the identification of primary risk drivers of salinity and quantification of the risks at sub-catchment scales to enable predictions spatially and under future scenarios for supporting evidence-based adaptive salinity management. In particular, a Hybrid Spatial Bayesian Network model (HS-BNM) is being developed to (1) integrate diverse data sources of different spatiotemporal resolutions and expert-informed knowledge, and (2) increase information learned by using data from multiple catchments. With inputs including monthly stream flow and salinity data, time-slices of land use mapping, recent hydrogeological landscape mapping, and long-term groundwater data, the model simulates monthly total dissolved solids. Based on the simulations, site-specific salinity risks are assessed according to their corresponding salinity threshold values required by associated water use purposes. Key results include the identification of key drivers of salinity variations across sub-catchments and predicting associated salinity risks under future scenarios of land use and climate forcing. Our findings also provide recommendations for future locations for monitoring and adaptive target-setting under future scenarios.

presentations.presentation_title: A Novel Deep Learning Framework for Enhancing Precipitation Nowcasting with GNSS-derived Precipitable Water Vapor
presentations.abstract: Accurate precipitation nowcasting is crucial for mitigating the impacts of extreme weather events. However, existing radar-based nowcasting methods primarily rely on a single data source and the kinematic extrapolation of radar echo motion, exhibiting limited capability to predict chaotic dynamics of convective systems due to the lack of supplementary atmospheric information. Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)-derived Precipitable Water Vapor (PWV) provides an integrated measure of atmospheric moisture and serves as a key precursor for precipitation evolution. Therefore, we introduce PWV as an essential physical constraint to improve precipitation nowcasting. This study presents WAVE-NowcastNet, a novel multi-source fusion deep learning framework that effectively integrates high-resolution radar observations with GNSS-derived PWV. At the core of the network design is the Water Vapor Control (WVC) module, which utilizes a trainable copy of the NowcastNet encoder and zero convolution layers. This design preserves skilful nowcasting capabilities of pre-trained NowcastNet while enabling the model to learn the modulating effects of water vapor on precipitation evolution. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that WAVE-NowcastNet consistently outperforms established baselines, including NowcastNet, Optical Flow, ConvLSTM, and PredRNN. Notably, our model achieves a significant performance leap in long-term forecasts (2–3 hours) compared to the original NowcastNet, with Critical Success Index (CSI) and Fractions Skill Score (FSS) scores increasing by 64.28% and 35.55%, respectively. Furthermore, WAVE-NowcastNet achieves the highest accuracy in areal rainfall estimation, highlighting its potential for enhancing downstream hydrological applications. This study also provides a scalable, computationally efficient paradigm for incorporating auxiliary atmospheric variables into deep-learning-based nowcasting models.

presentations.presentation_title: Environmental Controls and Alterations of Catchment Transit Times Across Space
presentations.abstract: Catchment transit time, the duration water takes to travel from precipitation to streamflow outlet, serves as a fundamental diagnostic of how river basins store, route, and transform water and solutes, and thus of how hydrological alterations propagate in river basins. In large river basins, transit times integrate the cumulative effects of climate variability, land-use change, topographic structrure, and groundwater-surface water interactions, yet existing knowledge remains fragmented across scales, regions, and methodologies. By synthesizing evidence from inter-comparison studies, we highlight two emergent insights relevant to hydrological alteration in large basins. First, dominant environmental controls on transit time exhibit scale-dependent shifts: transit times are most often associated with local soil and hillslope-riparian processes in small catchments, with topographic organization and hydrological connectivity at intermediate scales, and with groundwater-geologic mediation in large basins, while climatic condition modulates this transition by shaping catchment wetness. Second, transit time metrics show distinct sensitivities to environmental drivers; to our knowledge, this is the first synthesis to empirically reveal contrasting controls on different transit time metrics across studies. Despite methodological uncertainties, these observations potentially indicate valuable insights into how catchments partition rapid near-surface routing versus longer-term storage and mixing. This knowledge can provide a powerful lens for diagnosing hydrological alterations driven by climate change and human activities, including damming, water extraction, and land-use change, and for anticipating their ecological consequences through altered flow timing, water quality, and habitat connectivity. Further, we highlight key needs for further cross-catchment studies, including broader empirical coverage beyond small temperate catchments, improved tracer sampling across flow conditions, and uncertainty-aware, method-consistent analysis. Meanwhile, more systematic explorations are needed into complex interactions among environmental drivers, transport processes, and hydrological responses. These efforts will advance a process-based understanding of transit times, improving predictions of water and solute transport under environmental changes, especially in ungauged regions.

presentations.presentation_title: Hydrological Variability and Fish Community Responses in a Large Tropical Floodplain Lake
presentations.abstract: Large tropical floodplain lakes play a critical role in regional water resources and ecosystem services, yet their ecological responses to hydrological variability remain insufficiently documented due to limited long-term and integrated observations. The Tonle Sap Lake system, characterized by pronounced seasonal water-level fluctuations driven by monsoonal forcing and river–lake connectivity, provides a unique natural setting to explore hydrology–ecosystem interactions under various hydrological conditions. In this study, we present an integrated analysis of multi-season fish sampling data collected over two consecutive years under distinct hydrological conditions, combined with concurrent hydrological observations and analysis. Fish were captured using trap-based methods at multiple locations across the lake, and individual-level morphological information was obtained for a wide range of taxa. The dataset spans multiple seasonal phases, allowing comparative examination of fish community characteristics under different water-level regimes. We analyze patterns in fish size structure and community-level responses in relation to inter-annual and seasonal hydrological variability. Our results indicate that hydrological conditions are associated with shifts in the distributional properties of fish assemblages across seasons and years, while some structural characteristics remain comparatively stable. These results suggest that floodplain lake ecosystems may exhibit both sensitivity and resilience to hydrological variability, depending on ecological traits and temporal context. In addition to fish sampling, water quality measurements and environmental DNA (eDNA) samples were collected concurrently during the surveys, providing complementary background information on the lake system, although the present analysis focuses primarily on hydrological variability and fish community characteristics. By integrating hydrological information with biological observations, this study contributes to interdisciplinary efforts to better understand the coupled dynamics of water resources and aquatic ecosystems in large tropical floodplain lake systems under ongoing environmental change.

presentations.presentation_title: Recovery of Coastal Aquifers Under Changing Storm-surge Patterns
presentations.abstract: Storm surge results in vertical seawater intrusion into coastal aquifers, directly affecting the availability of fresh groundwater, which is a critical source of drinking and agricultural water for small islands. Climate change is expected to reduce the frequency of storm surges while increasing their intensity, resulting in complex challenges for the recovery of coastal aquifers to pre-surge conditions and for freshwater availability. Using integrated surface–subsurface numerical simulations of an idealized island aquifer, this study examines how shifts in storm-surge frequency and intensity control long-term groundwater salinization. The results identify two distinct long-term recovery regimes: full recovery, in which the aquifer returns to pre-surge conditions, and a shifted equilibrium, in which salt gradually accumulates and freshwater availability declines. The transition between these regimes is effectively captured by a dimensionless number, E, which links storm-surge characteristics and aquifer properties to cumulative salt loading. In the shifted-equilibrium regime, the excess salt load at the post-climate-change dynamic equilibrium is well approximated by a linear function of E. This framework offers a practical tool for the first-stage assessment of climate-change impacts on coastal groundwater systems, particularly for small islands with limited and vulnerable freshwater resources.

presentations.presentation_title: Migration Characteristics of Terrestrial Pollutants in Coastal Groundwater Reservoirs Under Thermal Effects
presentations.abstract: Coastal aquifers act as important hydrologic connection between terrestrial freshwater and oceanic seawater. They are inherently subjected to commonly found groundwater-seawater temperature contrasts and geological heterogeneity. However, the impact of these factors on land-sourced contaminant transport processes remains rarely understood, particularly in the presence of subsurface dams designed to control seawater intrusion. To address this gap, the study conducted both laboratory experiments and numerical simulations to investigate the complex transport dynamics of variable-density contaminants in a tidally-driven coastal subterranean reservoir. Spatiotemporal variation, transport pathways, spreading, residence time and solute mass fluxes were analyzed considering aquifer-ocean temperature differences as well as heterogeneous layering. Results found that as freshwater temperature decreases, the saltwater wedge contracts while the USP expands. This phenomenon is driven by thermally-induced changes in fluid density, viscosity and aquifer hydraulic conductivity. Compared to an isothermal scenario, warmer freshwater speeds up flow in the freshwater zone but slows down particle movement within the saltwater wedge. Conversely, colder freshwater dramatically decelerates contaminant transport and reduces a maximum mass discharge by nearly threefold. The lower-released contaminant is more susceptible to mixing with residual saltwater upstream of the subsurface dam, with average residence time prolonged by 1.8 times. The total efflux of the upper contaminant exhibits a distinct double-peak pattern due to the post-discharge behavior caused by the low-permeability layer. Measurable metrics through sensitivity analysis indicate substantial impacts of thermal forcing and aquifer permeability. These findings provide insights for better management of coastal groundwater resources in response to both natural and anthropogenic changes.

presentations.presentation_title: The Amazing Rhizosphere of Drylands – an Important Component of the Critical Zone
presentations.abstract: Drylands encompass diverse regions characterized by water scarcity that span hot hyperarid to alpine deserts with savannas intermediate to these extremes. Due to sparse vegetation cover and precipitation, drylands are vulnerable to climate change and poor land management. Key to the survival of vegetation in these stressed environments is understanding the functionality and interactions amongst water, soil, weathered bedrock, and nutrients that occur in the vadose zone and upper groundwater table. These processes play a major role in the translocation of essential solutes to the rhizosphere contributing to vegetation survival in drylands as well as influencing microorganisms in the rhizosheath. Typically, processes within the rhizosphere and the vadose have been viewed in isolation rather than holistically and are not applied at field scales nor incorporated into management practices and regional policies. Drylands pose special challenges because plant roots utilize water and nutrients from different sources each with their own microbiota. Here we highlight three typical dryland environments: (1) surface infiltrated water in shallow rooted vegetation; (2) capillary water accessed by deeper roots of shrubs and trees; and (3) groundwater and capillary water accessed by very deep woody tap roots of trees and desert shrubs. Ecosystems with shallow-rooted grasses, forbs, and succulents survive by infiltration during rainfall where nutrients, carbon, and microbial interactions are derived from surface soils. Deeper-rooted shrubs and trees can access the capillary fringe of relatively shallow groundwater where different pools of nutrients and microbes exist in weathered bedrock. And very deep-rooted trees and shrubs can reach groundwater reservoirs where much of the nutrient supply and microbiota exist and depend on geochemical weathering of the bedrock. Each of these dryland scenarios plays a unique role related to carbon sequestration and mechanical reinforcement of soils with profound implications for climate change adaptation, food security, slope stability, and erosion control.

presentations.presentation_title: Tracing and Integrating Water and Solutes Across Landscapes: Ecohydrological Applications from Inland to Coasts
presentations.abstract: Ecohydrology couples water and life. But ecosystems do not respond to “the water cycle” in general—they respond to the particular water they can access, and to the timescales on which that access changes. Tracers help because they turn hidden storage into legible history.I connect three studies that follow water from deep inland vadose zones, through soil-plant systems, to coastal-plain wetlands and aquifers—showing that the same question recurs across scales: who uses which water, and how fast is it replaced?On China’s Loess Plateau, bomb-peak tritium shows that mid-20th-century precipitation is still migrating meters below ground, implying decadal residence times in the deep vadose zone. That slow turnover matters because vegetation can run faster than recharge: deep roots can tap this reservoir, progressively depleting it and leaving persistent dried soil layers—an ecohydrological “debt” that is hard to repay.In a controlled isotope-labeling experiment, inferred mean transit times depend strongly on the transit-time model used (parametric versus data-based), especially for trees. Preferential flow and heterogeneity imply that plant water uptake can sample a biased subset of soil water, so “plant water age” need not equal “catchment water age.”On the coastal plain, stable isotopes and hydraulic time series show that wetlands and aquifers can be more connected than our conceptual models assume. In the Okefenokee–Upper Floridan system, mixing indicates substantial swamp-derived groundwater and water-level signals propagate downward with measurable lag, consistent with sustained vertical exchange.Together, these examples suggest a simple synthesis: ecohydrological change is often a storage problem before it is a flux problem. Multi-tracer evidence, interpreted through transit-time thinking, can diagnose when landscapes are buffered by subsurface memory, when they cross thresholds into disconnection, and where interventions are likely to matter for water resources and ecosystem services—from inland soils to coastal aquifers.
