presentations.presentation_title: Analysis of Runoff and Sediment Yield Reduction Effects According to Nbs Scenarios: a Case Study of the ‘cheoncheon Watershed’ in the Yongdam Dam Basin
presentations.institution: School of Advanced Science and Technology Convergence, Kyungpook National University
presentations.abstract: Approximately 70% of South Korea consists of mountainous terrain, where surface runoff dominates over infiltration during rainfall events. Under these conditions, the seasonal concentration of precipitation approximately 60% of annual rainfall occurring in summer combined with climate change induced increases in rainfall intensity and decreases in rainy days is expected to substantially increase runoff and sediment yield, thereby elevating the risk of human and material losses. As a mitigation strategy, this study evaluates the effectiveness of land cover conversion, a Nature-based Solution that utilizes natural processes and ecosystem functions, in reducing runoff and sediment yield. A soil erosion vulnerability map was generated using the Universal Soil Loss Equation to identify highly erosion-prone areas and establish land cover conversion scenarios. Design storms with 50, 100, and 200 year return periods following Huff’s third-quartile temporal distribution were applied to a physics-based distributed hydrological model, and peak and total runoff and sediment yield were compared between baseline and land cover conversion scenarios. The results indicate that peak runoff was reduced by 0.63–1.21% (50 year), 0.95–3.02% (100 year), and 2.85–5.03% (200 year), while total runoff decreased by 1.03–1.31%, 0.78–4.12%, and 3.01–3.82%, respectively, demonstrating flood mitigation effects. Notably, sediment yield exhibited higher reduction rates, with peak sediment yield reduced by 0.92–7.05% (50 year), 0.45–6.64% (100 year), and 1.77–11.97% (200 year), and total sediment yield reduced by 1.05–7.94%, 1.44–12.84%, and 2.23–12.35%, respectively. These findings confirm that land cover conversion exerts a pronounced influence on sediment yield reduction and represents an effective NbS strategy for mitigating runoff and sediment related flood risks.FundingThis work was supported by Korea Environmental Industry&Technology Institute(KEITI) through R&D Program for Innovative Flood Protection Technologies against Climate Crisis Project, funded by Korea Ministry of Environment(MOE)(2022003460002)

presentations.presentation_title: Applying Nbs to Shallow Mountain Wetland Restoration: Water Level Fluctuation and Habitat Reconstruction at Shuanglian Reservoir Wetland
presentations.abstract: Shuanglian Reservoir Wetland was originally a shallow mountain lake wetland characterized by natural seasonal water level fluctuations and diverse topography. However, anthropogenic modification in 1992 transformed it into a pond of uniform depth, resulting in a loss of shallow water zones. Furthermore, the introduction of invasive fish species by the public, which graze on aquatic plants, has severely inhibited the recovery of native vegetation. To address the intensifying impacts of extreme droughts and floods on the hydrology of the Critical Zone under climate change, this study proposes Nature-based Solutions (NbS) for habitat restoration.The proposed strategies include: 1. Local topographical modification to create shallow water zones and habitats of varied depths; excavated areas can also retain water during droughts to maintain wetland functions. 2. Planting dense tall-stemmed vegetation as biological barriers to exclude invasive fish from shallow zones, thereby promoting the germination of native aquatic plant seeds. Regarding hydraulic infrastructure, the existing facilities will be upgraded to remotely controlled electric tipping gates.An adaptive management strategy will be adopted. For the first three years, the current status (non-operation) will be maintained to establish an ecological monitoring baseline. The long-term goal is set to "minimal operation," utilizing a water balance strategy based on natural rainfall and groundwater seepage. This approach aims to maintain the rhythm of natural seasonal water level fluctuations—even under climate change scenarios characterized by drier dry seasons and intensified rainfall in wet seasons—serving as a reference for the restoration and climate change adaptation of similar shallow mountain wetlands.

presentations.presentation_title: Drought Propagation and Risk in Peninsular India: Assessing the Impacts of Climate Change
presentations.abstract: This study investigates meteorological drought synchronicity and propagation across nine major river basins in Peninsular India under climate change conditions and integrates the propagation characteristics within a drought risk framework. A complex networks-based approach is employed to track the drought propagation pathways. To identify meteorological droughts, the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) and the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) at a 6-month timescale are used, to capture both seasonal variability and longer-term climatic trends. For implementation, gridded observations from the India Meteorological Department (IMD) and historic simulations from 33 CMIP6 Global Climate Models (GCMs) for the period 1966–2014 are considered. Directed networks are established via event synchronization to map spatial pathways and categorize regions based on their role in drought transmission. By analyzing several network properties, such as in-degree, out-degree, and network divergence, the study identifies specific "source" regions that initiate drought signals and "sink" regions that are primarily influenced by external deficits. The results reveal a clear regional-based hierarchy in drought propagation among the nine river basins, with the basins located in central and eastern regions of the peninsular India (Godavari and Mahanadi basins) acting as dominant drought influencers. Conversely, basins located in the southeast and northeast regions (Pennar and Subarnarekha basins) function primarily as drought sinks. Furthermore, our analysis uncovers substantial differences between SPI and SPEI synchronization structures, highlighting the critical role of evapotranspiration in drought intensification and regional connectivity. Discrepancies between observed and GCM-derived networks emphasize model-dependent variability in simulating spatial drought dynamics. The network measures are further integrated into a risk framework combining exposure, sensitivity, and propagation strength to pinpoint areas at high drought risk. The findings demonstrate that complex network-based metrics provide a robust tool for identifying critical propagation hubs, thereby informing basin-scale water management and climate adaptation strategies in a warming world.

presentations.presentation_title: Identification of Agricultural Drought Propagation Sources and Sinks in Global Land Areas Using Event Synchronization
presentations.abstract: With the increasing population and the impacts of climate change, agricultural droughts are becoming a growing concern for ensuring future food security. Our ability to identify the regions vulnerable to agricultural droughts and undertake mitigation and adaptation strategies largely depends on our ability to properly assess the propagation of droughts. This study introduces an event synchronization approach to identify the sources and sinks of agricultural droughts and their propagation in global land areas. The sources are defined as locations where drought events predominantly originate, while sinks are locations where drought events tend to accumulate through propagation from other locations. For the analysis, the Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) soil moisture data for 1948–2024 at a spatial resolution of 1º x 1º are used. Mild to extremely severe agricultural droughts persisting for at least 3 months are identified using the standardized soil moisture index at each grid. Two events at the same or different grids are considered synchronized if the onset of an event occurs within 3 months following the onset of the preceding event. Directed drought propagation networks are constructed considering grids as nodes and establishing links based on event interdependence between grids. Several network measures, such as propagation strength, inward strength, and outward strength, are determined to identify the drought propagation sources and sinks. Results from this study show that high latitude regions, as well as extremely arid zones, such as the Sahara Desert, predominantly act as drought sources, whereas mid- and low- latitude regions, particularly those influenced by monsoon systems, act as drought sinks. The present results provide new insights into the interconnected nature of agricultural droughts.

presentations.presentation_title: Applicability Of The SR4DS Super-Resolution Model For Downscaling Of CMIP6 Rainfall Products In The Amazon River Basin
presentations.abstract: Driven by human activities, climate change is intensifying the hydrological cycle, resulting in significant changes in precipitation patterns and an increase in the frequency and severity of water-related disasters. Thus, assessing future climate-related disaster risks remains a major challenge, particularly at regional scales. In the Amazon River Basin, this limitation is especially pronounced due to the limited ability of Global Climate Models (GCMs) to represent complex tropical rainfall processes and their spatiotemporal variability. Reliable, high-resolution climate projections are essential for understanding the impacts of climate change and supporting effective mitigation and adaptation strategies. In this study, we evaluated the applicability of the Super-Resolution for Downscaling (SR4DS) deep learning model for simultaneously enhancing spatial resolution and reducing systematic biases in climate model precipitation in the Amazon River Basin. Daily precipitation products from four GCMs from the NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 dataset were downscaled from 0.25° to 0.05° (~5 km) resolution and assessed for both historical and future periods under the SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios. The results indicate that SR4DS improves basin-averaged precipitation variability across annual, monthly, and daily timescales, showing better agreement with observations relative to the original NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 products. In terms of the spatial distribution of rainfall, improvements are more evident at annual and monthly scales, while daily-scale performance remains limited. Overall, these findings highlight the potential of SR4DS to enhance rainfall representation in the Amazon River Basin, supporting its application in regional climate and hydrological studies. Funding: This work was supported by the Technology Innovation Program (RS202400398858, Development of AI-based urban flood damage risk prediction and evaluation technology for practical use) funded by the Ministry of the Interior and Safety (MOIS, Korea).

presentations.presentation_title: Bioinformatics-based Microbial Community Analysis Reveals Spatiotemporal Variability of Algal Blooms in Lake Taihu
presentations.abstract: Algal blooms have persisted in Lake Taihu for more than four decades, posing sustained risks to drinking-water security and overall water-supply quality. Previously, these blooms were typically dominated by Microcystis (phylum Cyanobacteria). Historically high eutrophication in Lake Taihu has provided favorable conditions for cyanobacterial proliferation. Meanwhile, climate change is reshaping the lake’s physical and biogeochemical environment in ways that can further promote cyanobacterial dominance, including rising air temperatures, increased solar radiation, and enhanced water-column stratification. Consequently, cyanobacterial blooms are expected to become more prolonged and spatially expanded. Over the past 20 years, local authorities have implemented a suite of nutrient-reduction and water-quality management measures. These interventions have contributed to measurable improvements in water quality, including declining concentrations of total phosphorus and total nitrogen, which are growth nutrient to Cyanobacteria. Under these changing conditions, the combined influences of climate change and ongoing water-quality recovery on Cyanobacteria blooms remain insufficiently resolved for Lake Taihu. In addition, cyanobacterial dynamics and their interactions with co-occurring bacterial communities are often obscured when bloom conditions are characterized solely using bulk indicators such as chlorophyll-a. To address these gaps, this study applies bioinformatics-based microbial community analyses to reveal the spatiotemporal variability of cyanobacteria and associated bacteria under contrasting water-quality states and environmental conditions in Lake. We collected monthly gene sequencing data of bacteria with physicochemical water quality indicators and meteorological parameters in Taihu Lake. We found that although lake-wide nutrient levels have declined in Taihu Lake, the northwestern embayment remains a hotspot of degraded water quality and elevated trophic status. Contrary to previous studies, Cyanobacteria did not exhibit a pronounced domination in summer or autumn but a seasonal shift in cyanobacteria dominance. Insight in such shifts in cyanobacteria dominance and the environmental drivers is important to expand water quality monitoring programs to secure water quality.

presentations.presentation_title: Hydropower Potential Assessment and Optimal Siting of Small Hydropower Integrated with Existing Water Infrastructure
presentations.abstract: As global demand for climate change mitigation and the expansion of renewable energy continues to increase, hydropower has attracted attention due to its high efficiency and stable power output. However, the development of large-scale hydropower projects is increasingly constrained by environmental impacts and limited local social acceptance, leading to growing interest in small hydropower utilizing existing water infrastructure as an alternative. The performance of small hydropower systems is strongly dependent on installed capacity: oversizing results in reduced operational availability under low-flow conditions, whereas undersizing prevents full utilization of the available generation potential. Accordingly, this study proposes a methodology to estimate power generation potential and to identify optimal development sites for small hydropower candidates linked to existing water infrastructure in Korea. Potential head locations were first screened using digital topographic maps. Subsequently, design discharge was derived based on the flow duration curve characteristics and effective head at each candidate site, and the expected power generation was assessed. In addition, realistic watershed-specific scenario data were generated to estimate site-level electricity generation, and a comparative evaluation was conducted to determine optimal development sites.

presentations.presentation_title: Enhancing Flood Resilience of a Large Catchment Using Hydro-ecological Based Wetland Management Approach Under Climate Change
presentations.abstract: Riverine flooding is intensifying globally due to climate change and land-use transformation, particularly in large monsoon-dominated river basins. Rising precipitation extremes have resulted in altered flood wave characteristics that are projected to substantially increase flood hazards. The degradation of natural ecosystems like wetlands also have contributed to elevate the flood risk. This study therefore presents an integrated assessment quantifying climate- driven changes in flood magnitude, inundation, and socio-economic exposure. Using downscaled CMIP6 climate projections across multiple SSPS and Global Warming Levels, GWL (1.5, 2, and 3 °C), this study projected a 10-14% rise in peak discharge by 2100 at major urban centres. These changes translate into substantial expansion of flood-prone areas, increasing agricultural inundation by ~1,200 km² and urban inundation by ~38 km². Although limiting warming to 1.5 °C reduces annual precipitation extremes by ~15% and peak discharges by ~9,000 m³/s, flood risk remains high due to persistent exposure and altered hydrological regimes. To address this elevated risk, the study evaluates rejuvenation and management of wetlands as a NbS for flood mitigation. The natural wetlands in monsoon climates often reach storage capacity early in the season and remain ineffective for high flows. Therefore, a hydro-ecological management framework was developed that enables partial storage release based on threshold precipitation conditions and ecological requirements. The proposed approach reduced peak streamflow at the catchment outlet by 1- 2% for existing wetlands and by up to 8% under maximum rejuvenation scenarios. At the sub-catchment scale, peak flow reductions reached ~30%, while the frequency of flood threat-level exceedances at major cities declined by up to 60%. These findings demonstrate that strategically managed wetlands can significantly enhance flood resilience and provide a viable, adaptive complement to climate mitigation and conventional flood-control measures.

presentations.presentation_title: Impact of Climate Change on Water Storage Requirements for Shallow-Rooted Crops in Hsinchu County, Taiwan
presentations.abstract: Shallow-rooted crops are defined by root systems primarily distributed within the top 30 cm of the soil surface. Due to their inability to access moisture from deeper soil layers, these crops are highly susceptible to drought. Common examples include leafy vegetables such as spinach, pak choi, and lettuce, as well as certain tubers like potatoes. To meet the high-frequency, multi-daily irrigation demands of these crops, irrigation systems are typically configured with water storage tanks for regulatory purposes.Using the Hsinchu region in Taiwan as a case study, this research utilizes water resource hazard indicators to analyze the rate of change in average annual Consecutive Dry Days (CDD) and investigates the resulting impact on water storage capacity under climate change. Statistical analysis from 2016 to 2024 reveals that CDD events of 5 to 10 days occurred more than five times annually. Over the past decade, 11 to 15-day CDD events were recorded in six separate years; 16 to 20-day events occurred in three years; and extreme events exceeding 21 days have emerged within the most recent two years.Projections for the rate of change in average annual CDD across three scenarios—RCP4.5, RCP8.5, and GWL2.0—show median increases of 4.78%, 7.43%, and 11.71%, respectively. Under the more severe GWL2.0 scenario, there is a 5% probability that the increase could reach 45.95%. These findings underscore the urgent need for adaptive water storage management to mitigate the risks posed by intensifying drought patterns.

presentations.presentation_title: Assessment of the Impact of Climate Change on the Hydrological Processes and Socioecological Systems
presentations.institution: Central University of Technology, Free State
presentations.abstract: Freshwater is fundamental to the functioning of ecosystems and to social and economic development. However, the availability of water resources and the integrity of freshwater ecosystems are increasingly threatened by climate change and associated extreme events. If not managed sustainably, these pressures can trigger complex and interlinked environmental, biophysical, ecological, and socio-economic challenges. Addressing such risks requires robust monitoring and evaluation systems, supported by real-time and rapid-response information for informed decision-making.This study examines the multifaceted impacts of climate change with a primary focus on strengthening the resilience of the socio-ecological systems of the Modder River catchment. It investigates the interactions among key environmental variables - particularly climate, surface water, groundwater, and soil processes - with the objective of developing sustainable adaptation strategies that can effectively mitigate climate-related impacts. A comprehensive understanding of soil–water–climate interactions is central to identifying long-term solutions that support freshwater sustainability and livelihoods within the catchment.To this end, hydrogeological and hydro-meteorological models are being developed and calibrated and subsequently integrated into a comprehensive scientific and technological framework for water security. The integrated modelling system will enable real-time monitoring, scenario analysis, and early warning capabilities, thereby supporting proactive water resources management and disaster preparedness. The approaches and lessons generated from this study are expected to be transferable to other catchments, with appropriate consideration of local contextual conditions.

presentations.presentation_title: Climate Change and Water Security: Assessment and Adaptation
presentations.abstract: Climate change has enormous consequences for our water resources, environment, health, and socio-economic development. With increasing population and improving living standard, demands for water in various sectors continue to rise, especially under projected climate change conditions, while the available water resources are limited. As a result, there are serious questions about our ability to meet our future water demands. Water security under future climate change conditions has become a common talking point in various sectors. Assessment of water security depends on reliable assessment of climate change impacts, evaluation of risks, and decision-making under uncertainty. This study aims to develop an integrated framework for the climate change-water security problem. The framework involves consideration of: (1) assessment of hydroclimatic extremes under climate change; (2) evaluating economic and social risks; and (3) decision making on adaptation strategies under uncertainty. The role of complex systems science theories, especially complex network theory, in developing such an integrated framework is discussed. The framework is implemented for several major river basins in India, with particular emphasis on drought conditions. The potential utility of this framework to study the broader water-energy-food nexus and security under climate change conditions is also discussed.

presentations.presentation_title: Hydrological Disaster-precipitation in Southeast Asia (1979–2023): Characteristics and Dataset Construction
presentations.abstract: Influenced by frequent extreme precipitation, Southeast Asia (SEA) is one of the most vulnerable regions to hydrological disasters worldwide. Disaster datasets constitute a fundamental basis for disaster-related research. However, statistical datasets for hydrological disasters in SEA remain relatively limited and are mostly archived in a tabular, event-based manner. That is, disaster records typically include location, timing, and impacts, but lack corresponding three-dimensional precipitation information. Therefore, establishing a hydrological disaster–precipitation dataset for SEA enables direct linkage between disaster events and precipitation information, facilitating studies on the evolution of precipitation characteristics and its disaster risk.Based on the above considerations, this study links hydrological disasters with their associated precipitation events by integrating the EM-DAT Disaster Dataset and CPC precipitation data, and constructs a SEA hydrological-disaster-related precipitation dataset for 1979–2023. Using this dataset, we analyze the composition, spatial distribution, temporal trends, and precipitation characteristics of hydrological disasters in SEA. The results indicate that hydrological disasters in SEA are dominated by typhoons, general floods, and riverine floods. Hydrological disasters in the region show an overall increasing trend. Although disaster response capacities of governments have improved since the beginning of the 21st century, resulting in a reduction of disaster-related fatalities, the overall impact of disasters has continued to intensify, as reflected by increases in both the total affected population and economic losses. The number of typhoon-induced disaster events has increased, suggesting an enhanced disaster-causing potential of typhoons in the region. Analysis of precipitation further shows that larger daily precipitation amounts tend to result in greater casualties and economic losses. The results obtained in this study establish a long-term, cross-national, and unified hydrological disaster dataset for SEA, providing data support for precipitation-related analyses of hydrological disasters and offering a scientific basis for disaster risk reduction and policy formulation.

presentations.presentation_title: Reconstructing Full-Grid Precipitable Water Vapor from Sparse GPS Observations using ConvLSTM-Inpainting for WRF Data Assimilation
presentations.abstract: Precipitable Water Vapor (PWV) plays a critical role in atmospheric processes and is one of the key variables for improving weather models through data assimilation. However, accurate PWV observations obtained from GPS-GNSS and radiosondes are spatially sparse, which limits their effectiveness in representing the full atmospheric moisture field required for weather simulation. Satellite observations from Himawari-8/9 provide continuous spatial coverage with infrared bands sensitive to water vapor (Band 08: near-surface, Band 09: mid-troposphere, Band 10: upper troposphere). Nevertheless, these observations do not directly provide total column PWV, requiring complex retrieval algorithms. To address these challenges, this study proposes a simpler total column PWV reconstruction framework using a Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory (ConvLSTM) Inpainting. The method integrates 512 point 3-hourly GPS-GNSS PWV observations with Himawari TBB Bands 08, 09, and 10, together with topographic constraints, to reconstruct full-grid PWV fields. The ConvLSTM Inpainting explicitly handles missing observations through masking and jointly learns PWV magnitude and temporal evolution, producing spatiotemporally consistent PWV fields that evolve realistically while reflecting terrain-induced moisture variability. The obtained full-grid 3-hourly total PWV is then validated against radiosonde and GPS-GNSS observations and subsequently assimilated into the WRF 4D-Var to assess their impact on precipitation forecasting. The simulations are conducted over western Japan (Kyushu, Chugoku, Shikoku, and Kansai) and compared with a control simulation and assimilation using 512 point-based GPS-GNSS PWV data. Results show that the reconstructed PWV improves heavy-precipitation forecasts, as indicated by higher critical success index (CSI) scores against Japan Meteorological Agency analysis precipitation compared to control run and point assimilation. In addition, the reconstructed PWV more accurately reproduces peak rainfall locations, indicating improved representation of moisture convergence and convective development. These results demonstrate the value of high resolution of PWV data is beneficial for enhancing moisture analysis resulting in improved precipitation forecast skill.

presentations.presentation_title: Understanding the Effects of Decadal Land Use Change and Climate Variability on the Water Balance of the Tonle Sap Lake
presentations.abstract: Serving as an important ecosystem within the Mekong River Basin, the Tonle Sap Lake experiences significant environmental changes due to the modifications of the Mekong River and the lake system. To understand the changing features of this system, a comprehensive assessment of water balance components is essential. This study evaluates a modified water balance model incorporating the contribution of hydrological alteration in tributary basins due to land-use change and climate variability to the lake volume change from 2001-2024. To quantify these impacts, we simulated tributary discharge using the SWAT model under four distinct scenarios including baseline, climate only, land-use only, and combined impacts. To accurately isolate tributary contributions, other components such as direct rainfall, surface evaporation, and Mekong mainstream flows were utilized consistently across all scenarios. The results indicate that annually, the Mekong River contributes 45% to lake storage, while tributaries and local rainfall contribute 44% and 11%, respectively. Conversely, 81.5% of lake storage is discharged back into the Mekong, with evaporation accounting for the remaining 18.5%. Analysis of tributary impacts reveals that climate variability reduced lake volume in May–June and a corresponding increase in December–January compared to the baseline. While land-use changes tended to enlarge rainy season volume and reduce dry season volume, the combined scenario mirrored the patterns of lake volume induced by climate variability in the tributary basins. The findings reveal that variations in inflow from the tributary basins have the potential to influence the volume of Tonle Sap Lake. Notably, climate variations have a more pronounced effect on volume changes than land-use alterations.

presentations.presentation_title: A Bayesian Framework for Estimating Z–R Relationship Parameters in Radar Rainfall Using Hybrid Surface Rainfall Data
presentations.abstract: Due to climate change, extreme rainfall events have increased, and precipitation patterns in South Korea increasingly exhibit short-duration, high-intensity characteristics. Weather radar systems provide spatially continuous rainfall estimates using empirical Z-R relationships; however, such estimates often show significant quantitative discrepancies compared to ground-based observations. Particularly, the Marshall–Palmer relationship underestimates rainfall in South Korea. Conventional deterministic correction approaches are limited in their ability to quantify the uncertainty associated with Z-R relationship parameters. To address these limitations, this study proposes a probabilistic framework based on Bayesian inference to estimate Z-R relationship parameters while accounting for parameter uncertainty. The framework was applied using Hybrid Surface Rainfall data and ground-based rainfall observations from Automatic Weather Stations in Seoul. Summer rainfall events during 2025 (June–August) were identified, and three rainfall events (low, moderate, high) were selected for analysis. For each event, Bayesian inference was used to estimate posterior distributions of the Z-R parameters, and the resulting rainfall estimates were compared with those from conventional Marshall–Palmer relationship. Model performance was assessed using statistical metrics. Results demonstrated improvements across all metrics for three rainfall cases, indicating that Z-R relationship parameters should not be treated as fixed values but should instead be dynamically estimated according to rainfall conditions. The findings highlight the importance of incorporating parameter uncertainty into radar rainfall estimation, particularly for intense rainfall events. Future work will extend this framework to mountainous regions to investigate the influence of topographic effects on Z-R relationships. presentations.presentation_title: Comparative Evaluation and Improvement of Empirical Solar Radiation Estimation Models Under Data-limited Conditions in Thailand
presentations.institution: Hydro-Informatics Institute (Public Organization), Ministry of Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation
presentations.abstract: Accurate surface solar radiation estimation is a fundamental pillar of hydrometeorology, serving as the primary energy driver for the water cycle through its influence on evaporation, transpiration, and soil moisture dynamics. While high-fidelity radiation measurements are often sparse, this study bridges the data gap by leveraging a dense network of over 3,000 National Hydroinformatics Data Center (NHC) stations managed by the Hydro-Informatics Institute (HII). These stations provide simple, real-time telemetry-meteorological data, offering a high-density alternative to traditional sensor networks for operational water management. We evaluated empirical solar radiation estimation models—including the Hargreaves–Samani (HS), Modified HS (M-HS), and Allen-1998 formulations—within a unified computational framework. To improve precision, the M-HS model incorporates daily variation of relative humidity and rainfall as surrogates for convective active cloud cover. Validation at a dedicated pilot-experimental site equipped with high-precision sensors indicates that the M-HS model significantly outperforms traditional formulations, reducing systematic bias to ~0.09 MJ m –2 day –1 and achieving a mean absolute error of ~2.70 MJ m –2 day –1 . Sensitivity analyses confirm that the refined model remains stable across the diverse seasonal changes and temperature fluctuations characteristic of Thailand’s climate. By integrating atmospheric variables with hydrological drivers through a high-resolution telemetry network, this study exemplifies the interdisciplinary blending of meteorology and hydrology required to enhance the accuracy of water balance modeling and flood-drought forecasting. The findings offer a practical, real-time solution for solar mapping and water resource utilization in data-limited environments.

presentations.presentation_title: Analysis of the Economic Effects of Urban Stream Restoration Using a Panel Hedonic Price Model
presentations.abstract: The economic effects of urban stream restoration are not confined to short-term premiums observed immediately after project completion; rather, they exhibit patterns of amplification or attenuation over time. However, prior studies in Korea have largely relied on single-year cross-sectional data, limiting their ability to adequately capture time-series changes before and after restoration. This study applies a hedonic price model to the Seoho Stream ecological restoration project in Suwon to quantitatively assess the economic benefits of stream restoration in terms of housing asset values. The hedonic price model incorporates housing and environmental attributes, including the number of rooms, distance between apartments and the Seoho Stream, and green space ratio, and model performance is evaluated using RMSE, MAE, AIC, and BIC. A semi-logarithmic specification is identified as the optimal model. The results indicate that the marginal willingness to pay (MWTP) for a 100 m decrease in distance between apartments and the stream increased by approximately 35% in the immediate post-restoration period (2016–2018) compared with the pre-restoration period (2013–2015). In contrast, MWTP declined by about 26% during the post-management phase (2019–2022) relative to the immediate post-restoration period. These changes in economic benefits closely align with trends in water quality indicators of the Seoho Stream (BOD, SS, and T-P), providing empirical evidence that environmental benefits capitalized into housing prices increased with water quality improvements following restoration but diminished as water quality subsequently deteriorated.

presentations.presentation_title: A Sequential 2-phase Physics-informed Machine Learning Framework for Spatiotemporal Error Correction in Grid-based Flood Modeling
presentations.abstract: Precise flood modeling is critical as climate change intensifies flash flood risks driven by extreme precipitation events. However, conventional grid-based physical models often suffer from spatiotemporal uncertainties arising from parameter estimation challenges and structural simplifications. To address these issues, this study proposes a hybrid grid-based flood model utilizing a sequential 2-Phase Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML) approach. The framework is divided into temporal (Phase 1) and spatial (Phase 2) correction stages. Phase 1 employs a PIML model trained on observed discharge, utilizing outputs from a lumped model and rainfall lag data to derive a Temporal Correction Ratio. Subsequently, Phase 2 utilizes a spatial AI model trained on Flood Risk Maps, taking flood depth from a distributed model and topographical factors (e.g., DEM, Slope) as inputs. During the hybrid simulation, the correction ratio from Phase 1 adjusts the grid-cell flow in the distributed model, and the resulting depths are refined by the Phase 2 model to generate final, sequentially corrected inundation maps. Validated in the Gyeongan Stream basin, Phase 1 significantly improved hydrograph accuracy, while Phase 2 successfully rectified inundation errors, aligning closely with official flood risk maps. By synergizing the interpretability of physical models with the non-linear capabilities of AI, this 2-Phase PIML framework offers a robust solution for enhancing the practical reliability of flood simulations.

presentations.presentation_title: A Physics-guided Deep Learning Emulator for Urban Flood Prediction: Integrating 1D–2D Hydrodynamic Information
presentations.abstract: Urban pluvial flooding can evolve rapidly during extreme rainfall, driven by tightly coupled interactions between surface runoff and sewer drainage. While physics-based high-resolution hydrodynamic models can accurately simulate urban flooding through coupled sewer–surface flow processes, their computational demands limit real-time prediction applications. Deep learning approaches can address this limitation by training emulators on high-resolution hydrodynamic simulations, enabling rapid predictions suitable for real-time applications. This study presents a physics-guided deep learning (DL) framework that emulates urban flood dynamics. To capture drainage–surface interactions in this framework, the model incorporates 1D sewer network data as auxiliary inputs alongside rainfall forcing, integrating 1D–2D hydrodynamic information. To represent local physical characteristics, the proposed architecture leverages static spatial features representing urban surface properties and sewer network configurations. Furthermore, various loss functions are compared to identify an optimal formulation for learning complex inundation patterns. The framework is applied to the Oncheon Stream basin in Busan, South Korea, which experiences frequent flooding. Results indicate that the proposed approach can substantially reduce computational burden while retaining key 1D–2D interaction signals, supporting fast forecasting for densely built, drainage-controlled urban basins.

presentations.presentation_title: Flood Water Level Prediction in Tidal River Reaches with Complex Boundary Conditions Using a Dual Encoder–decoder LSTM
presentations.abstract: Flood water level prediction in tidal river reaches is challenging due to the coexistence of multiple boundary forcings, such as dam discharges and tidal oscillations, which interact nonlinearly and vary in dominance along the river. Under such compound boundary conditions, conventional physically based hydraulic and hydrological models often exhibit structural limitations, including rigid governing equations and simplified boundary representations, thereby reducing their robustness for real-time flood forecasting. To address these challenges, this study proposes a Dual Encoder–Decoder long short-term memory (LSTM) model for flood water level prediction in tidal rivers with complex boundary conditions. The proposed architecture explicitly separates heterogeneous boundary forcings by treating dam discharge and tidal level as independent time-series inputs. Each input is processed through a dedicated encoder to capture its distinct temporal dynamics, and the extracted latent features are integrated in a decoder to predict flood water levels. Rainfall is incorporated as an auxiliary input to support flood event characterization. The model was applied to the Namgang Dam–Gahwa Stream system in South Korea, where dam releases predominantly control upstream water levels at Yusugyo Station. In contrast, downstream levels near Geomjeong-ri are strongly influenced by tidal forcing. Ten historical flood events were analyzed, with eight used for training and validation, and two for independent testing. Model robustness was further evaluated using K-fold cross-validation. Results show consistently high predictive performance at both upstream and downstream stations. For lead times of 1–3 hours, Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency values exceeded 0.8 for all flood events. The dual encoder–decoder framework effectively reproduced proportional upstream flood responses to dam discharges and complex, nonlinear water-level variations driven by dam–tide interactions downstream. Overall, the results demonstrate that explicitly disentangling complex boundary conditions using a dual encoder–decoder LSTM provides an approach for flood water level prediction in tidal river systems.

presentations.presentation_title: LSTM Model with Transition Zone for Soft Sensing of River Flood Water Levels
presentations.abstract: Accurate estimation of river water levels during flood events is essential for flood warning and river operations, yet the predictive performance of data-driven models often differs substantially between normal-flow and flood-flow conditions. Dual-model long short-term memory (LSTM) approaches that separately train models for low- and high-water-level regimes can improve regime-specific performance. However, when combined using threshold-based hard switching, these models may produce unstable predictions near the regime boundary, as small fluctuations in upstream water levels can trigger frequent model toggling. This study proposes a Dual-Model LSTM with a Transition Zone for robust soft sensing of river flood water levels. Two LSTM models are independently trained for low- and high-water-level regimes, with the regime threshold defined by the mean upstream water level at the Hoemunri station. Instead of selecting a single model output, a transition zone [T-δ, T+δ] is introduced, where T=124.70 m and δ=0.05 m. Within this zone, the final water level estimate is computed as a convex combination of the two model outputs, with blending weights that vary continuously according to the real-time upstream water level, enabling smooth regime transitions while preserving regime-specific model strengths. The proposed framework is evaluated in the Seomjin River Basin, South Korea, using observations from September to October 2024 that include both normal-flow and flood conditions. Across two test cases, the transition-zone approach achieved high overall accuracy (NSE = 0.970–0.987) while improving robustness near regime boundaries. In Test #2, RMSE decreased from 0.0287 m to 0.0266 m (approximately 7.3%), and NSE increased from 0.9704 to 0.9745 compared to hard switching. These results demonstrate that the proposed transition-zone-based dual-model LSTM provides a stable and regime-aware soft sensing framework, supporting reliable continuous estimation of river flood water levels for operational monitoring.

presentations.presentation_title: Performance of a Parallel LSTM with Varying Lead Times for Urban River Flood Water Level Forecasting
presentations.institution: Dankook University, Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering
presentations.abstract: Urban river flood water level forecasting is a critical component of flood response and disaster management, where reliable predictions across varying lead times are essential for effective early warning. However, conventional LSTM-based multi-step forecasting approaches often experience performance degradation as lead time increases due to error accumulation, temporal discontinuity, or increased computational burden. These limitations are primarily associated with forecasting structure rather than data availability, highlighting the need for structurally robust prediction frameworks. This study evaluates the performance of a Parallel Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model for urban river flood water level forecasting under varying lead-time conditions. The proposed Parallel LSTM architecture divides the overall forecasting horizon into multiple sub-intervals that are predicted in parallel, while sharing hidden state information between adjacent blocks to preserve temporal dependency and continuity in the predicted time series. This structural design aims to mitigate instability commonly observed in long lead-time forecasts. The model was applied to the Tancheon Basin, an urban watershed traversing the metropolitan areas of Seoul and Seongnam, focusing on water level observations at the Daegok-gyo and Gungnae-gyo gauging stations. Multi-step flood water level forecasts were conducted for lead times ranging from 10 to 360 minutes using nine historical flood events. The forecasting performance of the Parallel LSTM was systematically compared with conventional Direct (multi-output) and Recursive forecasting structures. The results indicate that the Parallel LSTM consistently maintains stable predictive performance across all lead times, achieving Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) values exceeding 0.87 even at extended lead times. In contrast, the Direct and Recursive approaches exhibit a gradual decline in performance as lead time increases. These findings demonstrate that the Parallel LSTM provides a robust and effective forecasting structure for urban river flood water level prediction under varying lead-time conditions.

presentations.presentation_title: Integrating Machine Learning and Tomographic Modeling to Characterize Groundwater Dynamics and Heterogeneity
presentations.abstract: Understanding groundwater dynamics and subsurface heterogeneity is essential for sustainable water resource management, yet the complexity of subsurface processes and the simplifying assumptions of many traditional models remain significant challenges. Long-term monitoring of groundwater levels, pumping and recharge operations, and rainfall using dataloggers is now common, producing large volumes of high–temporal-resolution data. However, these datasets are often simplified for modeling and not fully utilized.In many cases, monitoring data have sufficient temporal resolution to support data-driven modeling using machine learning to quantify groundwater responses to varying hydraulic stresses across aquifer units. This presentation introduces a novel Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) framework for estimating groundwater response functions from monitoring data. Unlike previous studies that use LSTM and other machine-learning methods to directly simulate groundwater levels, this framework is formulated within a transfer function–noise context by customizing the loss function to explicitly represent system response behavior. The estimated response functions are validated through convolution with pumping time series using monitoring data from multiple water agencies in Southern California and are shown to be more robust and physically realistic than conventional predefined response-function shapes.The presentation further demonstrates how these response functions can be integrated into tomographic inverse modeling to delineate the spatial distribution of hydraulic conductivity. A model predictive covariance matrix of head responses is constructed, and non-redundant information is extracted via spectral decomposition into eigenmodes. Only eigenmodes associated with the largest eigenvalues, representing the dominant predictive variance, are retained for inversion. A Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) method is employed to enable robust parameter sampling. An application to an environmental site in Arizona illustrates the effectiveness of the proposed AI-enabled model and data integration framework.

presentations.presentation_title: A Study on the Credibility of Flood-inundation Location Identification from Social Media Data
presentations.abstract: Social media data have been increasingly used in flood disaster management because of their large volume, timeliness, and low acquisition cost. However, their application is constrained by significant uncertainty in data quality. To address this challenge, this study proposes a framework for assessing the credibility of flood-inundation locations extracted from social media (FLLSs). Considering flood formation mechanisms, the proposed framework enhances the application quality of social media data in flood disaster emergency management. First, the most probable inundation coordinate is identified from multiple geocoding candidates associated with each ambiguous location name. Second, the credibility of FLLSs is quantified using a combined weighting method based on multi-source indicators. Finally, an interpretable machine learning approach is employed to analyze the relationships between assessment indicators and FLLS credibility. Results show that the proposed framework effectively addresses the geocoding problem, achieving a 22.81% improvement in flood location identification accuracy. FLLS credibility significantly improves the performance of flood risk zone identification using social media data. Rainstorm factors and topographic wetness index play dominant roles in determining FLLS credibility. In addition, notable spatial inequality is observed in social media attention to flood events, with urban areas receiving substantially more coverage than suburban and rural regions. These findings indicate that social media data should be integrated with other data sources to achieve a more comprehensive and reliable analysis of flood disasters.

presentations.presentation_title: Dynamic Parameterization of the Target Storage Method Improves Reservoir Operation Modeling
presentations.abstract: Reservoir outflow plays a critical role in water-resources management and hydrological modeling, yet its prediction remains challenging because reservoir operations are strongly influenced by human decision-making and increasingly disrupted by extreme hydroclimatic events. Machine-learning approaches, particularly long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, have been widely applied to reservoir outflow modeling due to their high predictive skill; however, their lack of physical interpretability remains a major limitation. Traditional physically based reservoir models, on the other hand, often show substantially poorer performance. Here we demonstrate that a physically based target storage method, when equipped with dynamically varying parameters, can achieve performance comparable to—or even exceeding—that of purely data-driven LSTM models. We employ LSTM networks to learn time-varying parameters required by the target storage formulation through a differentiable parameter-learning framework. The approach is evaluated using around 100 reservoirs across the continental United States. Compared with a standalone LSTM benchmark (median Kling–Gupta Efficiency, KGE = >0.9), the target storage model shows a dramatic performance improvement when dynamic parameterization is introduced: the median KGE increases from 0.566 under static parameters to 0.915 when all parameters are allowed to vary in time. Notably, we find that allowing only a single parameter to vary dynamically yields performance comparable to the fully dynamic configuration. This result highlights the effectiveness of dynamic parameterization in enhancing reservoir model performance while preserving physical interpretability. Overall, our findings suggest that dynamically parameterized physical reservoir models offer a promising pathway to bridge the gap between physically based and machine-learning approaches for reservoir outflow prediction.

presentations.presentation_title: The Long Road to Medium-precision CO₂ Observation Networks in Alpine Environments: Limitations of Physical Corrections and Dominance of Instrument Drift
presentations.abstract: High-altitude regions like the Tibetan Plateau lack high-resolution atmospheric CO₂ observations. Although Open-Path Eddy Covariance (OPEC) systems are widely deployed, their data are frequently discarded due to severe systematic biases (±20–50 ppm) caused by harsh environmental conditions. We investigated the physical origins of these biases using collaborative experiments with LI-7500A and IRGASON systems on the Tibetan Plateau.Unexpectedly, traditional physical error corrections cannot explain the primary observational biases. Pressure measurement artifacts caused by thermal pressurization resulted in only minor underestimations (0–3 ppm). Furthermore, even in low-temperature and low-wind environments, the density error induced by instrument surface self-heating is negligible (maximum correction 0.8 ppm), suggesting self-heating effects can be disregarded in such environments.After removing physical artifacts, a substantial residual bias (∼ -20 ppm) remained. We confirmed that "Non-linear Instrument Thermal Drift" is the dominant error source. This drift exhibits distinct "morning-evening asymmetry" and varies by instrument design. Consequently, we proposed a "Three-Component Decoupling Model" emphasizing empirical drift correction, which successfully converged biases to a medium-precision level. This study highlights the limitations of physical corrections in alpine environments, identifying instrument drift as the primary obstacle, and provides a technical pathway for transforming legacy OPEC networks into "Medium-Precision CO₂ Monitoring Networks."

presentations.presentation_title: Snow Cover Change on the Tibetan Plateau Based on Modis and Ims Products
presentations.institution: Tibet Institute of Plateau Atmospheric and Environmental Sciences
presentations.abstract: Snow cover plays a critical role in the global energy and water cycles. Snow cover on the Tibetan Plateau (TP) provides vital water sources in western China and Himalayan regions, in addition to its weather and climate significance. In this study, the spatial distribution and topographic controls of snow cover on the TP are examined based on snow cover frequency (SCF) derived from MODIS snow cover product (MOD10A2 v5) and digital elevation model (DEM) data. The spatial and temporal variations of number of snow cover days (SCD) on the TP from 2004 to 2021 are further analyzed based on the daily NOAA IMS 4 km snow and ice products.The results show that (1) snow cover on the TP is spatially unevenly distributed and is characterized by rich snow and high SCF on the interior and surrounding high mountain ranges, with less snow and low SCF in inland basins and river valleys. Snow cover on the TP presents elevation dependence. The annual mean SCF below 3000 m is less than 4% and it reaches 77% above 6000 m. (2) Annual mean number of SCD on the TP is 71.1 days, with winter at 27.2 days, followed by spring (22.1 days), autumn (14.5 days) and summer(5.3 days). (3) Over the past 17 years from 2004 to 2021, the number of SCD on the TP has shown a significant increasing trend, with an increase of 11.5 days decade -1 . Spatially, the number of SCD mainly showed an increasing trend in the high-altitude areas in the central and eastern parts of the plateau, while it mainly showed a decreasing trend in the high-altitude areas in the south and northwest.

presentations.presentation_title: GEWEX Research Activities in Central Asian Mountains
presentations.abstract: Since the early 1990's the Global Energy and Water Exchanges (GEWEX) core project of the World Climate Research Programme (WCRP) has been active in Asia and its mountainous regions. Starting with the GEWEX Asia Monsoon Experiment (GAME) followed by various other large scale regional endeavours. In this presentation an overview is given of past research successes followed by potentual future avenues. Given the geopolitical changes and constraints new ways of collaboration need to be developed to support climate and water research in the region. In particular, open science, data sharing as well as observational capacity development deserves attention.

presentations.presentation_title: Seasonal Variation of Subsurface Water Dynamics in Rainfall-runoff Processes in a Headwater Catchment in Northern Japan Alps
presentations.abstract: We monitored an alpine headwater catchment on Mt. Norikura to clarify the seasonal variation of rainfall-runoff characteristics. Two adjacent small watersheds, NR1 (0.14 km 2 ) and NR2 (0.11 km 2 ) with the altitude from 2550 to 2980 m and the temperature from -20 to 20 °C, were observed from July through September 2025. Stream runoff and electrical conductivity (EC) were continuously monitored, and stream water was sampled daily to analyze dissolved silicate (SiO 2 ) concentrations and stable isotopes. Seasonal snow patches disappeared by mid-September in NR1 and by mid-July in NR2. During the post-snowmelt period, stream runoff occurred only during rainfall events in NR1, whereas it occurred perennially in NR2, although at a lower level than during the snowmelt period. The runoff ratio to the rainfall in NR2 (100.8%) was much higher than that in NR1 (29.5%). The SiO 2 concentration in stream water in NR2 was higher than that in NR1. Additionally, the d-excess of stream water decreased throughout the observation in both watersheds, reflecting low rainwater value and high snowmelt water value, and was higher in NR2 than in NR1 during the post-snowmelt period. These results indicate that the influence of subsurface water on stream runoff is greater in NR2 than in NR1. During rainfall events exceeding 40 mm, in NR2, stream EC rapidly decreased and recovered in the snowmelt period, whereas the EC recovery lagged behind the runoff recovery in the post-snowmelt period, indicating that rainwater contributes to the stream runoff for a longer duration after rainfall in the post-snowmelt period than in the snowmelt period. Consequently, these results indicate that groundwater may flow across topographical watershed boundaries, sustaining the stream runoff in NR2, and its flux should decrease from the snowmelt to the post-snowmelt period. This seasonal change in groundwater flow could influence the event water flushing processes in NR2.

presentations.presentation_title: The Impact of Rain-on-snow on Runoff Generation and Compound Flood Risk in the Alpine Watershed Under the Changing Climate
presentations.abstract: Rain-on-snow (ROS) events are becoming increasingly significant drivers of hydrological change and heightened flood risks in alpine watersheds under global warming. This study focuses on the Manas River Basin in the northern Tianshan Mountains of Xinjiang, China. Utilizing a SWAT hydrological model calibrated with both runoff and snow water equivalent (SWE), we simulate future ROS conditions using outputs from 24 CycleGAN bias-corrected NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 climate models under four SSP scenarios. Combined with a multivariate Copula analysis framework (MvCAT), we systematically evaluate the spatiotemporal evolution of future ROS events, the contribution of different runoff generation mechanisms to extreme runoff, and the compound risk of ROS-induced flood events. The results show an overall decline of projected SWE shows with earlier snowmelt onset. The frequency of ROS events tends to increase across most subbasins, notably in mid-to-high elevations, with occurrence projected to rise by 8–20 days during the far-future period and advance by 5–40 days; Analysis of the top 1% runoff events reveals distinct elevation controls: rainfall-driven runoff dominates in low-elevation areas; mixed runoff contributes most in mid- to-high elevation zones but declines with warming; snowmelt-driven runoff prevails at high elevations. Shifts in dominant runoff generation mechanisms are more pronounced in the far-future period than the near-future; Copula analysis indicates a positive correlation between ROS days and days with runoff exceeding the historical 90th percentile threshold (Q90). This dependence slightly intensifies under higher emission scenarios and lower elevation bands, indicating significant elevated future compound flood risks triggered by ROS.

presentations.presentation_title: Evaluation of Clear‑cutting in Riparian Zones in Japan for Flood Damage Reduction
presentations.abstract: This study assessed the effectiveness of sequential clear-cutting of channel vegetation to reduce flood damage in Japan’s first-class rivers. Additionally, it identified river systems with high potential for both climate change adaptation and mitigation through vegetation removal. Channel vegetation data were derived from the normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) obtained via Sentinel-2 satellite imagery. Corresponding roughness coefficients were assigned based on vegetation characteristics to conduct flood inundation simulations.The flood inundation model incorporated flood discharge values corresponding to various return periods, enabling the calculation of inundation depths across affected areas. Economic damage estimates were derived from inundation depths for each land use category, following the guidelines outlined in the Flood Control Economics Manual. These estimates facilitated the computation of annual expected flood damage for both vegetated and non-vegetated conditions in each river system. Biomass potential was estimated by multiplying NDVI values by the vegetated area within the river channels.The results indicated that the flood damage reduction effect of channel vegetation clear-cutting varied depending on the sequence of removal. While clear-cutting generally reduced flood damage in many watersheds, certain areas had increased damage due to enhanced flood propagation downstream, resulting from reduced upstream inundation. A correlation was observed between the effectiveness of vegetation removal and the population within the watershed. The Tokachi, Yubetsu, and Iwaki Rivers were identified as systems where clear-cutting of channel vegetation would be particularly effective in achieving both adaptation and mitigation objectives.

presentations.presentation_title: Evaluation of Flood Control Options Based on Urban Flood Inundation Simulations in Toyama City, Japan
presentations.abstract: Recently, urbanization has increased rainfall runoff, and the progress of global warming has led to frequent torrential rains and flood disasters. To address these increasingly severe and frequent water disasters, an integrated basin management for a flood control called as “River Basin Disaster Resilience and Sustainability by All” is being promoted in Japan. Few studies evaluate these flood control options and urban flood adaptation measures based on inland flood simulations in an urban area. Therefore, this research conducted inland flood analysis and evaluated watershed flood control options in Toyama City, Japan. The results confirmed a damage reduction effect, with flooded areas reduced by up to approximately 38%

presentations.presentation_title: Future Projection of River Water Temperature Using Practical Stream Temperature Model
presentations.institution: Civil Engineering Research Institute for Cold Region
presentations.abstract: River water temperature is a crucial ecological indicator, and the projected warming associated with climate change is a matter of considerable concern. The process of simulating river water temperature based on the heat budget equation necessitates the integration of two distinct sets of data. The first set encompasses meteorological data such as radiation, air temperature, and wind speed. The secondary set consists of river-specific data, including flow rate and water depth. The incorporation of these variables is imperative for accurate and reliable simulations. However, the difficulty in collecting appropriate input data also makes simulation using heat balance models difficult. The present study developed a practical water temperature estimation model capable of predicting water temperatures using only air temperature and flow rate. Utilising this model, we conducted a comprehensive assessment of historical water temperature fluctuations and projected future increases under future climate conditions. Furthermore, the effectiveness of water temperature reduction measures involving controlled discharge volumes and discharge temperatures from dams was quantified.

presentations.presentation_title: How Does Adaptive Capacity Shape Flood-induced Wealth Inequality? Insights from a Coupled Human-water Dynamical Model
presentations.abstract: Floods disproportionately impact low-income households, exacerbating poverty and inequality. While wealthier households often experience floods as temporary setbacks, poorer households frequently become trapped in long-term cycles of loss and slow recovery. Although prior studies attribute these divergent outcomes to differences in adaptive capacity – assets, learning, agency, organization, and flexibility – the mechanisms through which specific components shape post-flood wealth trajectories and recovery remain poorly understood. This study addresses this gap by examining why high-income households recover rapidly from repeated floods, whereas low-income households do not. We develop a dynamic human–water coupled model that links flood hazards, household wealth evolution, and multiple dimensions of adaptive capacity across income groups. The model is empirically grounded in original household survey data from two communities (both flooded and non-flooded) in the Philippines and informed by an extensive literature review, enabling it to capture local knowledge and observed recovery behaviors while minimizing assumptions. Model validation is conducted using historical flood events and household wealth trajectories across income strata. Results reveal that adaptive capacity components exert highly heterogeneous effects on recovery outcomes. Assets, learning, agency, organization, and flexibility contribute with different relative weights to recovery speed and future loss reduction. Scenario experiments demonstrate that strengthening targeted adaptive capacities among low-income households substantially improves recovery rates and mitigates long-term wealth erosion. These findings provide policy-relevant insights for designing targeted interventions that enhance resilience, reduce inequality, and prevent disaster-induced poverty traps in flood-prone developing regions.

presentations.presentation_title: The Risk of Model Transferability: Evaluating Flood Model Reliability Before and After Flood Control Investments (FCI)
presentations.abstract: Structural flood control investments (FCI), including levee construction and river improvements, play a key role in flood mitigation. These interventions can modify river morphology and flood characteristics, underscoring the need to update flood models following FCI implementation. This study investigates the risk of model transferability that occurs when pre-FCI calibration parameters are applied to post-FCI events. We address two critical questions: (1) to what extent do hydrologic parameters shift following major FCI? and (2) how significant is the difference in flood risk and damage estimation when using non-updated models? We utilize the Water and Energy Budget – Rainfall Runoff Inundation (WEBRRI) model applied to the Marikina Watershed, Philippines, an area that underwent extensive FCI following the catastrophic 2009 Typhoon Ondoy. The model was validated against a robust dataset including reported flood levels from household interview surveys (n = 912) and flood inundation maps generated through local government geotagging efforts during three major flood events (2009, 2020, and 2024). The results show that failing to update parameters leads to errors in estimating flood depths and economic losses. This study provides evidence that implementing FCI projects must be followed by flood model’s recalibration to maintain accuracy in disaster planning. We conclude that without continuous model updates, the structural FCI intended to protect cities can lead to a false sense of security due to inaccurate risk data. This research supports the need for maintaining reliable flood management systems in rapidly changing urban environments.

presentations.presentation_title: Urban Heat Island Mitigation Through Green Infrastructure: Insights from the Hanoi Metropolitan Area, Vietnam
presentations.abstract: Rapid urbanization in tropical regions has intensified the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect, creating mounting environmental and public health concerns. This study investigates how the Urban Green Spaces (UGSs) mitigate thermal stress in the Hanoi Metropolitan Area, Vietnam, under different land cover and climate warming scenarios. A five‑year composite (2020–2024) of Landsat 8 Land Surface Temperature (LST) data was analyzed in conjunction with the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Relative Surface Evapotranspiration Index (RSETI), and Normalized Difference Built‑up Index (NDBI). Buffer‑zone analysis showed that UGS can lower summer LST by up to 2.14 °C within 100 m, with cooling effects fading beyond 800 m. Future thermal dynamics were projected using the Random Forest (RF) model to simulate land cover and climate warming scenarios. Results reveal that a 10% increase in vegetation cover reduces summer LST by 0.56 °C, while a 10% decrease raises it by 0.58 °C. Yet, under a +1.5 °C warming scenario, these local cooling benefits are negated, producing a net summer LST rise of 0.94 °C. The Urban Thermal Field Variance Index (UTFVI) analysis highlights vulnerability thresholds. Vegetation expansion improved thermally comfortable zones from 50–55% to 60–65% under current conditions, but under +1.5 °C warming, even maximum greening could not sustain baseline comfort levels, with stressed zones expanding to 55–60% of the urban area. Overall, the findings demonstrate that while local green infrastructure remains effective under moderate warming (+1 °C), broader regional climate mitigation strategies are essential to counteract stronger warming scenarios.
presentations.session_title: Climate Change Impacts on Regional Hydrological Issues: Beyond Adaptations and Mitigations

presentations.presentation_title: Preliminary Study on the Mechanisms and Implications of Annual Precipitation Extremes in Mainland China
presentations.abstract: Xima in Yunnan is the site with the highest recorded annual precipitation in mainland China based on long-term observations. However, the multi-scale formation mechanisms of its extreme precipitation and its indicative significance for large-scale climate events remain unclear. This study aims to investigate the formation mechanisms of extreme precipitation in Xima and explore its physical linkage with major flood events in the Yangtze River Basin. Using long-term precipitation observations from the Xima station in Yunnan (1979–2021), flood records in the Yangtze River Basin, and ERA5 reanalysis data, differences between typical major flood years and climatic mean states across various scales are compared. The study indicates that the formation of extreme precipitation in Xima results from the synergistic effects of multi-scale systems. On the large scale, Xima lies along a key pathway of moisture transport from the South Asian monsoon via the Bay of Bengal. Its unique flared terrain induces stationary, intense convergence at the 850 hPa level. Topographic uplift and blocking significantly enhance precipitation. Further analysis reveals that during major flood years in the Yangtze River Basin, such as 1998 and 2020, the atmospheric circulation exhibited an anomalous pattern characterized by a westward and intensified subtropical high and a deepened Indian low. This configuration not only significantly enhanced moisture convergence and precipitation intensity in the Xima region but also strengthened moisture transport toward the Yangtze River Basin. Xima serves as a critical node linking the Bay of Bengal moisture source with precipitation in the Yangtze River Basin. The intensity of its precipitation extremes can indicate the strength of the South Asian monsoon and anomalously high precipitation during the Meiyu period in the Yangtze River Basin, holding potential indicative value for assessing South Asian monsoon activity and predicting flood risks in the Yangtze River Basin.

presentations.presentation_title: Integration and Application of Hydrometeorological Coupled Forecasting Technology
presentations.abstract: With the frequent occurrence of extreme rainstorm events, the frequency and intensity of hydro-meteorological disasters in river basins are continuously increasing, making the demand for hydro-meteorological technology increasingly urgent. At the same time, numerical forecasting and fine-grid precipitation forecasting are becoming more and more reliable, providing a solid technical foundation for the development of hydro-meteorological technology. The Institute of Heavy Rain in Wuhan has conducted extensive explorations and attempts in the field of hydro-meteorological research, resulting in technical achievements in the following aspects:(1) Three different spatial resolutions (3km × 3km, 9km × 9km, and 27km × 27km) of forecast rainfall were coupled with a distributed hydrological model for flood forecasting experiments. The experimental results showed that although the forecast rainfall of the three spatial resolutions could not predict the rainfall distribution consistent with the actual situation, in some cases, when the temporal and spatial distribution errors of rainfall were offset, more accurate flood forecasting results could still be obtained. (2) A hydrological forecasting technology based on precipitation ensemble forecasting has been designed and established. By inputting different precipitation forecast information into hydrological models, different flood inflow process curves can be obtained. Compared with single and deterministic precipitation input information, the application of precipitation ensemble forecasting products in hydrological forecasting can provide more precipitation forecast information than deterministic forecasting. (3) Based on existing technological achievements, a real-time hydrological and meteorological forecasting system for river basins has been developed. The system accurately predicted the flow and water level of many large reservoirs and main stream stations in the large-scale flood disaster forecast of the Yangtze River basin in 2020, and the relevant forecast results were reported to the Ministry of Science and Technology.

presentations.presentation_title: Roles of Terrain in the Convection Initiation of an Extreme Rainfall Event Along the Eastern Slope of Wushan Mountain, China Under a Weak Synoptic Forcing
presentations.abstract: The roles of terrain in the convection initiations (CIs) under a weak synoptic forcing remain unclear. This study first analyzes the spatiotemporal distribution of CIs and their weather circulation patterns near the complex terrain of the Wushan Mountain from 2016 to 2020 through statistical analysis, concluding that the eastern slope of the Wushan Mountain is a hotspot for CIs and that convection is more likely to be triggered under weak weather forcing conditions. Then, take an extreme rainfall event in the eastern slope of Wushan mountain on 25 July 2019 resulted from a linear convective system originates from the mergence of several convective cells triggered along the eastern slope of Wushan mountain as an example, the influence of the topographic thermodynamic and dynamic forcing on the afternoon (15:00−16:30 BJT) CIs associated with this event has been systematically studied. Results show that the CIs occur in highly unstable and moderate wind shear environments and are closely correlated with the acceleration of upstream low-level southeasterly winds, which are induced by the superposition effect of the large-scale pressure field and meso-scale thermally forced mountain-plains solenoid (MPS) circulation. The large-scale pressure field accelerates the low-level southerly winds by increasing the northward pressure gradient force, while the meso-scale MPS circulation in the afternoon strengthens the low-level easterly winds by increasing the westward pressure gradient force. As the upstream airflows are accelerated, the strong convergence uplift due to the topographic dynamic blocking triggers new convections in the transition region from blocked to unblocked flows. The numerical sensitivity experiments further highlight the key role of the thermodynamic forcing of Wushan mountain in the low-level airflow acceleration and CIs.

presentations.presentation_title: Quantitative Precipitation Estimation Algorithms and Improvements Based on Fengyun Satellite Data
presentations.abstract: Quantitative Precipitation Estimation (QPE) algorithms were developed using meteorological satellite data from FY-4 and FY-3. The QPE products generated by the algorithms were evaluated, and based on the evaluation results, the algorithms were optimized and improved. Firstly, leveraging the statistical relationship between cloud top brightness temperature and surface precipitation, the QPE algorithm based on FY-4 observation data was constructed using information on brightness temperature and brightness temperature difference between two bands in the near-infrared and infrared bands. Methods such as brightness temperature variability and dynamic time integration were adopted to improve the algorithm, which significantly alleviated the underestimation of heavy precipitation and overestimation of light precipitation, with the root mean square error (RMSE) decreased from 13.78mm to 10.04mm, and the mean error (ME) reduced from -8.48mm to -1.40mm. Taking full advantage of microwave detection's ability to penetrate cloud clusters, the least squares method was used for precipitation retrieval from the brightness temperature data observed by the FY-3G Microwave Radiometer Imager (MWRI). The results showed that the products generated by this improved algorithm had smaller biases, with the ME decreasing from 0.717mm/h to 0.549mm/h and the RMSE dropping from 5.056mm/h to 4.431mm/h. Conducting QPE using satellite data with wide coverage is helpful for obtaining accurate areal rainfall information, providing important data support for hydrological model forecasting and other applications.
